title: How OneDrop Adapts to Each Platform
text: I originally built OneDrop to send files from Edge. On a phone I could keep the same message list and composer, but opening a file needed different handling. On my computer I want to open the downloaded file. In Edge on my iPhone I want the system share sheet so I can choose which app receives it. Part one and part two cover storing messages in OneDrive and syncing them across devices. Here I’m using OneDrop 1.0.3 again to look at the changes needed for desktop Edge, mobile Edge and the standalone iOS app. # Shared code across platforms # App entry points and shared packages OneDrop’s entry points live under apps/ . Edge on desktop and mobile uses the same extension, while the standalone iOS app has its own entry point. The UI, message model and OneDrive operations used across platforms live under packages/ . Directory Purpose apps/edge Desktop side panel, mobile extension pages and adaptations for Edge on iOS apps/ios WebView entry point and Swift plugins for the standalone iOS app packages/ui React message list, composer and settings screens packages/core Message model, settings types and runtime request protocol packages/platform Interfaces the UI uses to access platform features, plus the runtime dependencies for OneDrive operations packages/app-runtime Application services for sign-in, device settings and downloads packages/extension-runtime Background request dispatch and entry point handling for the Edge extension packages/onedrive Reading and writing message chunks, archives and attachments through Microsoft Graph packages/web-storage IndexedDB storage for cached data, pending tasks and download records # Reading the current month’s messages Every version of OneDrop loads the React UI from packages/ui . To read the current month’s messages, for example, the message list sends this request: const response = await sendRequest({ type: "messages/read-current-month" });Each entry point installs its own PlatformBridge before loading the UI. This bridge receives requests from the UI and passes them to the appropriate handler. The request names, parameters and response types are all defined in packages/core . The Edge extension passes the request to its background process with browser.runtime.sendMessage . The handler gets the current UTC month and calls readMonthDocument() to fetch the messages. The standalone iOS app uses Capacitor to load the same UI in a WebView. It has no extension background process. Its bridge handles the request inside the app, gets an access token from the native authentication plugin and passes it to readMonthDocumentWithAccessToken() to read the same month. Both paths use the monthly message reader in packages/onedrive . The UI receives the same messages/month response and can display it with the same list component. That leaves just one place to change the rules for reading message chunks. # Edge extension entry points and layout The extension chooses its entry point using the platform information reported by Edge and the browser’s user agent. # The desktop Edge side panel When the side panel API is available, OneDrop configures the toolbar icon to open the message list beside the current page. I can keep the page I’m reading open and drop text or files into the composer next to it. # The OneDrop tab in Edge on Android Tapping OneDrop in Edge on Android opens a separate android-mobile.html tab. If that tab is still open, tapping the icon again brings it back into view. # The popup in Edge on iOS Edge on iOS uses the ios-mobile.html popup. The extension manifest also declares the desktop side panel page, so that entry point checks the platform too. If Edge loads the panel on iOS, it switches to the mobile styles and the iOS Edge bridge. # When the mobile keyboard opens On mobile, the message composer sits at the bottom of the page. Tapping it brings up the keyboard and reduces the visible area. The page needs to shrink with that area to keep the composer above the keyboard. The popup in Edge on iOS gets the visible area through the browser’s visualViewport . Its height is the available height and offsetTop is the distance from the top of the layout viewport. When the visible area changes size or position, OneDrop writes both values to CSS variables. The popup’s root element uses them to adjust its height and position: top: var(--ios-edge-popup-offset-top, 0px);height: var(--ios-edge-popup-height, 100dvh);The height can keep changing while the keyboard animates into place. After the composer receives focus, the popup updates its dimensions several times over the next half second and calls scrollIntoView({ block: "nearest" }) on the still-focused input to keep it on screen. # Account and device settings # Sign-in windows and token storage When I click sign in in the Edge extension, OneDrop uses the browser’s identity.launchWebAuthFlow to open Microsoft’s authorisation window and receive the callback. If the browser doesn’t provide that method, the extension completes authorisation in a temporary tab. Once signed in, it stores the tokens in browser.storage.local . Part one covers the authorisation code exchange. The standalone iOS app has its own sign-in path. Tapping the same button calls the Swift plugin OneDropAuth through Capacitor. The plugin starts an ASWebAuthenticationSession to display Microsoft’s sign-in page. After sign-in, iOS returns the result to the plugin through the app’s registered callback scheme. The plugin checks that the callback’s state matches this sign-in attempt, exchanges the authorisation code for tokens and stores them in the iOS Keychain. When the UI needs to read OneDrive, it asks the plugin for an access token. The plugin also refreshes it when it approaches expiry. # Per-device settings These devices can share a Microsoft account and still keep their own settings. Each installation generates a device ID and saves its display name and preferences in settings/devices/<device-id>.json . When I replace a phone and remove the old device from the list, OneDrop removes its settings. Messages and attachments sent from that phone still follow the deletion and recovery rules in part two. # Attachment actions Suppose I send a file from my computer and tap the message on another device. Each platform receives the same OneDrive file identifier, driveItemId . What changes is where the file goes and how I can open it. The UI reads PlatformCapabilities to find the actions available on the current platform and decide which buttons to show. # Downloads in desktop Edge Desktop Edge saves files through the browser’s downloads API. It also supports Save As and showing a file in its folder. OneDrop remembers the browser download ID for each attachment. When I open the same attachment again, it can look up that ID and open the file if it’s still there. Part one describes how OneDrop confirms a download has finished. # Downloading attachments in Edge on Android In Edge on Android, the download starts from the OneDrop tab. When I tap download, the extension prepares the attachment URL and navigates to it with location.assign() , handing the file to Edge. The page follows the task and associates the completed browser download ID with the attachment. If I leave the page during a download, it can use the saved task state to check on the download when I return. # Sharing files in Edge on iOS Edge on iOS needs a browser File object before it can share an attachment. OneDrop looks up the attachment in IndexedDB using its driveItemId . It checks the cached name, recorded size and actual size of the binary data. A match lets it prepare the file straight from the cache and skip the download. If the cache can’t supply the file, OneDrop asks the background process for a download URL and reads the response stream, counting bytes as each chunk arrives. The progress indicator takes the total size from the Content-Length header when available, falling back to the size in the message. If the attachment has a known size greater than zero, OneDrop checks the final length before caching it. Once the file is ready, OneDrop checks that the browser can share it with navigator.canShare() , then calls navigator.share() to open the system share sheet. I can choose which app receives the file there. On the first tap, OneDrop downloads it before attempting to share. With a usable cached copy it can open the share sheet straight away. # Previewing and exporting files in the iOS app On the same iPhone, the standalone app can download an attachment to local storage through a Swift plugin. It uses URLSession to download the file into the app’s Documents directory and records its location by driveItemId . If the name is taken, the plugin saves the new file under a numbered name. When I tap Open, the plugin checks that the file still exists and asks UIDocumentInteractionController to present a system preview. I opened the same dog photo I shared from Edge earlier. The system preview shows its filename, IMG_4566 , at the top. To save the photo somewhere else, I can return to the attachment menu and choose Save as. The plugin opens the iOS document picker so I can choose a folder for the copy. # Copying an image To paste a photo into a chat, I can choose Copy image from the OneDrop attachment menu once the image preview has loaded. The shared UI takes the preview data, converts it to PNG and passes it to the current platform to write to the clipboard. The Edge extension wraps the PNG data in a ClipboardItem and calls navigator.clipboard.write() . In the standalone iOS app, Capacitor passes the image data to the Swift plugin, which decodes it into a UIImage and assigns it to UIPasteboard.general.image . I can then paste the photo into another app that accepts images.

title: OneDrop Storage and Multi-Device Sync (Part Two)
text: Part one covered authorisation, the storage layout and file transfers. What happens after a message has been saved? This part follows it through concurrent edits, history, deletion and recovery. The implementation described here is still OneDrop 1.0.3. # Synchronisation, conflicts and archives # Reading messages and using the cache # When a client syncs Clients pull changes when the interface opens, comes to the foreground, refreshes manually or needs to read data as part of sending. There’s no server of mine continually pushing updates. Once the browser closes, you can’t treat it as an always-online messenger. On returning to the foreground, the UI checks the time since the previous sync. This avoids rereading the month every time you switch windows. Normal mode checks after 30 seconds, Reduced mode after five minutes. Manual mode doesn’t trigger a sync from this foreground check. # Reading a month and reusing cached chunks The client lists files under messages/YYYY-MM , requests 200 items per page, follows @odata.nextLink and reads the chunks in numerical order. The 200-item limit applies to a single listing request. It doesn’t limit the number of messages or chunks in the month. A missing monthly directory is a valid empty state; a failed request is an error. Pagination URLs are checked against the expected Graph API scope. The cache stores more than the merged list. For each chunk it retains the DriveItem ID, ETag, parsed document and message line numbers. An ETag identifies the version returned by the server. If the version matches and line information is present, the cached document can be reused. Changed chunks are downloaded and parsed, up to three at once. A growing history doesn’t mean downloading every JSON body on every refresh. In the code below, a matching version and complete line information let OneDrop reuse the local record. Otherwise it calls downloadDocument() . const downloaded = cached?.eTag === item.eTag && cached.messageLines ? { document: cached.document, messageLines: cached.messageLines } : await downloadDocument(item.id, month, accessToken);After parsing, OneDrop merges by ID, sorts by createdAt and ID, and applies deletion markers from tombstones . Identical records with the same ID collapse to one. Different contents for a single ID produce a conflict record with source files and line numbers so the choice can be resolved later. # Following an upload in progress Part one introduced the file-uploading placeholder. Other devices can see it before the attachment finishes. To pick up the final file message promptly, the visible, signed-in UI polls after waits of 2, 5, 8 and 10 seconds, then continues at 10-second intervals. Once the accumulated waits reach 120 seconds it ends the round and marks outstanding placeholders unresponsive. That total counts time spent waiting between requests, excluding the requests themselves. If the attachment is already stored and the local record is committing , the client retries the final message on the same schedule, stopping at the round limit. An online event attempts those commits again and cleans up placeholders left by failed uploads. This work resumes from local state when the client is running or connectivity returns. # Loading earlier messages Scrolling back expands more batches within the loaded months and fetches one earlier UTC month. Each read carries a request version and a local write version; the client checks both before applying the response so a stale read can’t overwrite a newer local action. It also remembers a visible message as a scroll anchor. When older items arrive above it, the message you were reading stays in view. # ETags and concurrent writes Reads can merge several chunks, but a write has to protect each chunk against concurrent changes. Suppose A and B both read version v1 . A adds a message and writes successfully. If B now writes back a full JSON document built from its old copy, it can erase A’s message. # Check the version and retry When updating an existing chunk, OneDrop sends the ETag it read in If-Match . The server accepts the write only if the version still matches. After A’s update, B’s condition no longer holds. A changed file can produce 412 Precondition Failed ; competing object creation can produce 409 Conflict . For these responses OneDrop invalidates the cache and retries from the cloud: if (response.status === 409 || response.status === 412) { await deleteMonthCache(month); snapshot = undefined; continue;}The next iteration reads a fresh snapshot, merges by message ID and decides where to write. If the ID is already present it returns the existing result, avoiding a duplicate append on a retried send. After five unsuccessful rounds it reports the conflict so the caller can retain the failure state. A new chunk has no previous ETag, so OneDrop asks Graph to fail if the name already exists. If two devices both try to create 0002.json , one succeeds. The other rereads the month before deciding where to write. If a directory has been deleted and Graph returns 404, OneDrop clears the corresponding cache and tries to locate the directory again. # Network failures and local write ordering A network error has different semantics. The server may have committed the request even if the client never received its response. The write function invalidates the cache and reports the error without automatically replaying the write. A subsequent sync or explicit retry can inspect the message ID to determine what happened. Within one runtime, a Promise queue serialises modifications to monthly messages. Operations across devices still depend on server-side conditional writes. Keeping the queue at the message-write layer also means a large attachment needn’t block text messages for the entire duration of its upload. # Chunking and damaged records # Choosing a chunk A single ever-growing monthly JSON file would make every append more expensive. OneDrop tries the last active chunk first. If the proposed append exceeds the 256 KiB soft limit, it starts a new chunk. The final document has a separate 320 KB hard limit, and chunk numbers stop at 9999. Exceeding those limits is an error; reaching the numbering limit seems unlikely for message metadata alone. The soft limit decides when to roll over. The hard limit applies to every final chunk, including a new one or an existing one after a placeholder is replaced. Older chunks remain readable. Committing a file message requires finding the chunk that contains its placeholder, regardless of which chunk is now last. The code first merges the message into the last chunk to measure the result. If it exceeds the soft limit, OneDrop starts a new chunk and checks its size against the hard limit before writing. # Corruption and conflicting contents A read can collect malformed JSON and conflicting records while still displaying the readable remainder. A strict read aborts. Treating invalid JSON as an empty list would lose the distinction between damaged and genuinely empty data. An ordinary append can proceed while leaving a damaged file untouched. The next chunk number accounts for damaged chunks so their paths won’t be reused. After rereading the remote month, a known conflict for the target message ID blocks the write. The cached fast path means there isn’t a complete remote conflict scan before every write. Archiving is stricter: any damaged source file or conflicting message blocks consolidation. When two versions have the same ID, silently keeping the last one read could discard the other version. Instead, the user chooses which source to retain. resolveMessageConflict() removes the record from the other source chunks with ETag checks. If another device edits a source in the meantime, the user must recheck it before the earlier decision can be applied. # Archiving history # Building and verifying the archive Once a UTC month has been over for more than 24 hours, OneDrop can consolidate it into archive/YYYY-MM.json . The delay gives end-of-month writes some breathing room. Subsequent history reads can then fetch fewer files. Eligible history reads try the archive first. If there is no archive, the read fails, or it takes more than eight seconds, they fall back to the source chunks. Current tombstones apply to archive reads too. Creation uses conflictBehavior=fail so an existing archive won’t be overwritten. After writing, OneDrop reads it back and compares the serialised result with the intended document. If an archive already exists, its contents must match the visible source month. Damaged files, unresolved messages or an inconsistent existing archive leave the task blocked. # Retries and timeout reporting Task state is persisted locally. cooling-down waits for the next retry, auth-paused waits for authorisation, blocked needs a data problem resolved, and succeeded records success. Ordinary retries wait five minutes, thirty minutes, six hours and then twenty-four hours. Reopening the interface doesn’t immediately repeat a task known to be failing. After thirty seconds the task can report a timeout. That notification doesn’t cancel the underlying operation. The client still waits for its actual outcome, so a later success can update the task state. # Source cleanup and recovery limits A successful archive leaves the monthly source directory in place initially. The task saves a digest of the archive and sets cleanupPending . Cleanup rereads the raw archive and checks that digest before trying to remove the source directory. A failed cleanup can be retried independently. The check returns early if the archive is missing, there’s no saved digest, or the digest no longer matches. There is a limitation here: the digest verifies the archive, but the implementation doesn’t check that the source still matches its archived version immediately before deletion. Another device could have changed the source since the archive was created. The archive also contains visible messages after tombstone filtering. It doesn’t preserve every original deleted record. Cleaning the source directory can therefore remove the only remaining recovery source for a deleted message. Recovery has to check what still exists. # Deletion, recovery and physical cleanup # Tombstones and retention Removing a message from a local array would let the next sync bring it back. Removing it from one chunk still leaves the possibility of a stale writer. OneDrop records deletion separately as a tombstone , and all read paths apply the same deletion state. A tombstone records messageId , originalMonth , deletedAt and optionally recovery . It’s saved by original month in tombstones/YYYY-MM.json . Monthly and archive reads filter the matching IDs. Hiding a message therefore doesn’t require its attachment and original JSON to disappear at the same instant. The monthly read below fetches the set of deleted IDs and excludes them from the merged result. It leaves the source files in place. const deletedMessageIds = await readTombstoneIds(month, accessToken);const messages = unfilteredMessages.filter( (message) => !deletedMessageIds.has(message.id),); Updating and removing tombstones also use read, merge and conditional write, with up to five attempts on conflict. Otherwise deleting one message on A could overwrite a deletion marker B had just added for a different message. The deletion action records its recovery policy: disabled, 3, 7, 10 or 30 days, or forever. Finite retention can include an explicit recoverableUntil . For older records without the information, cleanup falls back to ten days after deletion. Disabling recovery makes the record eligible immediately; remote objects still go through the cleanup process. # The recycle bin and restoring messages A tombstone stores deletion state, not a full copy of the text or attachment. For the recycle bin, OneDrop reads the raw archive and unfiltered records in the source chunks, merges them and looks for the matching ID. A hidden message can appear there while its original content remains available. Identical records can merge. Contradictory versions with the same ID don’t count as one unambiguously recoverable message. If the source is gone, the client doesn’t construct a placeholder from the tombstone and present it as recoverable. Restore checks the tombstone and original again, removes the marker, then clears the monthly cache. If either the tombstone or the original is missing, the restore function returns an error here. Otherwise, the next normal read includes the message. There’s no new message ID or attachment upload. Retention defines cleanup eligibility; it isn’t an independent backup. A manually removed original or a source lost during archive cleanup can’t be reconstructed from an ID. Even an intact file message doesn’t guarantee the attachment is still there: external operations can move or delete it. # Cleaning up expired data # Selecting eligible items A separate cleanup process removes remote attachments and metadata. Automatic scans run at 24-hour intervals and inspect up to twenty eligible items per round. A manual cleanup skips the normal interval, expiry wait and ordinary round limit. Automatic scans skip permanent retention; disabled recovery is eligible from deletion time. The code below calculates the earliest cleanup time as eligibleAt . Automatic scans skip records that haven’t reached it, while manual cleanup skips that time check. Before deleting anything, the client reads the source and checks the month implied by the message timestamp. If it can’t identify the record uniquely, it stops processing that item. An absent record alongside a damaged file warrants investigation: an empty set of successfully parsed records doesn’t prove cleanup is complete. # Checking references and deleting in order For a file message, the client checks whether another undeleted message in the currently read month refers to the same driveItemId . If it does, it keeps the attachment. Otherwise it locates files/year/month/message-ID , verifies that it’s a folder containing the target DriveItem , and only then deletes that attachment folder. This check doesn’t build a global reference index over all of OneDrive. After handling the attachment it removes metadata from message chunks or the archive. JSON rewrites use ETags. A change or conflict defers the operation and leaves the tombstone for later. The marker is removed last, once the metadata step is confirmed, and the item is marked complete. An intermediate state is possible: the attachment is gone but a conditional metadata update hasn’t succeeded yet. A local maintenance queue serialises restore and cleanup on one device; it doesn’t lock every device. A subsequent restore must still recheck its sources. Two other cases are worth distinguishing. A failed local send that never reached the cloud can be removed from IndexedDB after confirmation, without creating a cloud tombstone . A file the user has already downloaded to a system directory is their own copy. Cleaning up its message or deleting its download registration doesn’t delete that local file.

title: OneDrop Storage and Multi-Device Sync (Part One)
text: My introduction to OneDrop covers the project, installation and future plans. This two-part series looks at the implementation. Here I’ll follow Microsoft account authorisation and the path a text or file message takes through storage, upload and download. Part two covers multi-device sync, conflicts, archives, deletion and recovery. Using OneDrive saves me from deploying and maintaining a storage service. It still leaves the client responsible for message state. Two devices can edit the same record, an upload can finish before its message commits, and a deletion has to reach other devices. This diagram shows the entry points, shared UI and storage in OneDrop 1.0.3. # Microsoft accounts and OneDrive authorisation # The client authorisation flow OneDrop queries, reads and writes OneDrive files through Microsoft’s API, Microsoft Graph. Both the Edge extension and the standalone iOS app run on the user’s device. Microsoft handles login and file requests. Here “extension” refers specifically to the browser distribution; “client” includes the native app as well. # Authorisation with PKCE Requests go directly from the client, so the first step is to get the user’s authorisation. A distributed extension or app can’t keep a server secret confidential. OneDrop uses the authorisation code flow with PKCE. The user signs in and grants consent on Microsoft’s page, then the client exchanges an authorisation code for tokens. The client generates a random verifier , hashes it with SHA-256 and Base64URL-encodes the digest as a challenge . The authorisation request sends the challenge . The token request later supplies the original verifier alongside the code. The server checks that the digest matches the challenge from this authorisation. Possession of the code alone is insufficient to complete that exchange. The 64 in the code is the byte count before encoding. The request declares code_challenge_method=S256 . A separate random state is returned unchanged in the callback, allowing the client to match the response to its login attempt. Missing code, mismatched state or an authorisation error stops the exchange. # Registering the application and setting its configuration For a custom build, register an application in Microsoft Entra. Entra is where Microsoft manages sign-in and authorisation settings. Registration identifies the application requesting sign-in. Released builds already contain their application configuration; users sign in with their own accounts. The client needs three settings. Client ID identifies the application. In Entra ID → App registrations, create or open the application and copy Application (client) ID from Overview. This identifies the registration, independently of the user’s account or password. Authority selects the sign-in endpoint and account audience. OneDrop defaults to https://login.microsoftonline.com/common . To support work, school and personal Microsoft accounts, the registration must also allow those account types; select the multitenant option that includes personal accounts. Redirect URI tells Microsoft where to return the result. Register it under Authentication. The URI sent in the request must match. This is a client callback address, unrelated to OneDrive’s file directories. Desktop Edge supplies extension identity APIs for generating the callback, opening an authorisation window and receiving its result. Android Edge also uses an extension callback but may fail to create the window. In the implementation described here, iOS Edge lacks Identity API and needs a web callback. When available, browser.identity.getRedirectURL("auth") returns an address such as https://<extension-id>.chromiumapp.org/auth . Before a client ID is configured, OneDrop’s setup screen displays the Redirect URI to register. Copy it from your own installed extension; different packages can have different IDs. Without that API, the default web callback is https://onedrop.sycamore.top/auth.html , registered as a single-page application (SPA). If you host another callback, change both the local configuration and the Entra registration. Set the build values in .env.local at the project root: WXT_ONEDROP_ENTRA_CLIENT_ID=your-application-client-idWXT_ONEDROP_ENTRA_AUTHORITY=https://login.microsoftonline.com/common# Web callback for browsers that cannot generate an extension callback URLWXT_ONEDROP_TAB_REDIRECT_URI=https://onedrop.sycamore.top/auth.htmlRestart the development server and reload the extension after editing. Microsoft documents app registration and client account audiences. # Requesting permissions OneDrop includes the following scopes in its login request: const SCOPES = [ "openid", "profile", "offline_access", "https://graph.microsoft.com/Files.ReadWrite",] as const; openid requests identity information so the client can obtain an ID token . profile requests basic profile details such as the name and username shown in the UI. offline_access requests a refresh token so an expired access token can be replaced without another interactive login. OneDrive still requires network access. Files.ReadWrite requests file access on behalf of the signed-in user. Add it under API permissions → Add a permission → Microsoft Graph → Delegated permissions. The application acts as the user rather than independently of one. Microsoft defines the scopes and the user or organisation must grant them. See the OpenID Connect scope documentation. The delegated file permission extends beyond Apps/OneDrop . The application confines its normal operations to that directory through its own code; creating a folder doesn’t narrow an already granted permission. # Login windows and session state # Authorisation window or temporary tab Desktop Edge prefers browser.identity.launchWebAuthFlow , with a callback from getRedirectURL("auth") . If that API is absent or reports that it cannot create a browser window, OneDrop opens a temporary tab instead. Register the callback actually used by the build. When launchWebAuthFlow is unavailable, the client persists state , verifier , callback and start time. On a later status check it can see whether the tab reached the callback and finish the exchange. Interactive login allows the user to act in the sign-in window. Silent login tries to reuse an existing session. Pending authorisation data is retained for five minutes; interactive login waits five minutes and silent login thirty seconds. These limits govern a login attempt, independently of the lifetime of the resulting access token . # Token roles and storage The access token authorises Graph requests, the refresh token obtains new access tokens, and the ID token carries identity claims. The extension stores its tokens in browser.storage.local : closing the sidebar can leave the background runtime suspended, so it must be possible to resume without a permanently running process. Native iOS uses Keychain, as described in the platform notes. # Refreshing tokens and signing in again getCurrentAccessToken() checks validity before Graph access, allowing a 60-second expiry margin. As expiry approaches, it uses the refresh token to request a new access token . The refreshInFlight ??= in the screenshot lets concurrent callers share that refresh Promise . That avoids duplicate refresh requests and races when saving the responses. The promise is cleared on completion so a future refresh can start. Ordinary refresh failures return an error. For errors such as invalid_grant or interaction_required , OneDrop first tries silent authorisation with prompt=none . If that also cannot proceed it clears its stored tokens and requests login. Signing out of OneDrop clears its own tokens without signing the browser out of Microsoft. The UI decodes name and username using readUnverifiedIdTokenClaims . As the name indicates, it reads the fields without verifying the signature locally. These values supply display information, and the username can serve as a silent-login login_hint . # The Apps/OneDrop directory Messages, attachments and settings live in one predictable location visible to the user in OneDrive. After obtaining a token the client checks /me/drive/root:/Apps/OneDrop , relative to the signed-in user’s drive root. A 404 indicates a missing directory. It checks and creates each level as needed, first Apps , then OneDrop . Creation fails on conflict; if another device created the folder first, the client rereads it rather than replacing the object. Overwriting an object with the same name could destroy content the other device had already written. Part two uses similar reasoning for writes and archives. # Storing and transferring text and files # Separating metadata from attachments # Cloud layout Text and files appear in the same message list but are stored differently in OneDrive. Text is small enough to store in JSON. File contents are uploaded separately; their message records store what’s needed to locate and display them. Here’s the layout, using example years and months: Apps/OneDrop/├── messages/│ └── 2026-10/│ ├── 0001.json│ └── 0002.json├── archive/│ └── 2026-09.json├── files/│ └── 2026/10/<message-id>/<original-filename>├── settings/│ ├── account.json│ └── devices/<device-id>.json└── tombstones/ └── 2026-10.jsonmessages contains active chunks, archive holds consolidated months and files contains attachments. Device settings have separate documents under settings , avoiding a shared rewrite for every preference change. Reads use the ID markers in tombstones to filter deleted messages. UTC month boundaries keep devices in different time zones from assigning the same timestamp to different months. # Message fields and validation OneDrop uses Zod to define the message schema and validate the JSON it actually reads. TypeScript types alone can’t check an incoming document. The common fields are the format version schemaVersion , a UUID message identifier id , the creation time createdAt and an optional senderDeviceId . Stable IDs identify the original across retries and merges. The sender device ID distinguishes messages from this installation from messages sent on other devices. It identifies an installation, not the Microsoft account. const messageBaseSchema = z.object({ schemaVersion: z.literal(1), id: z.uuid(), createdAt: z.iso.datetime(), senderDeviceId: z.uuid().optional(),});Text extends the common fields: export const textMessageSchema = messageBaseSchema.extend({ type: z.literal("text"), text: z.string().trim().min(1).max(20_000),});The text is trimmed, must remain nonempty and is limited to 20,000 characters. File messages include attachment.driveItemId , filename, size and MIME type, with optional image dimensions and thumbHash . A DriveItem represents a Graph file or folder; a MIME type such as image/png describes its content. The UI can show the name, size and an image placeholder before fetching the object by ID. Each chunk has its own schemaVersion , month and messages array. Both the chunk and its individual records are validated when read. Users can edit, move or damage files outside OneDrop. Writing a file once doesn’t guarantee it will still match the schema when OneDrop reads it again. For images the client tries to read the original dimensions and generate a ThumbHash, a compact encoding of a blurred preview. It prefers createImageBitmap , falls back to a local image object, scales proportionally to a longest side of at most 100 pixels and reads RGBA from a temporary canvas. Only the preview canvas is downscaled. The original attachment is uploaded unchanged. If metadata extraction fails the send continues without the optional preview. # Local pending tasks Draft text, files waiting to upload, commit state and attachment details needed for retries have to survive a closed UI or a suspended Manifest V3 service worker. OneDrop saves pending text and pending transfer records in IndexedDB, the browser’s local database. A Blob holds the file bytes for retries. putPendingTransfer() writes a record, getPendingTransfer() retrieves one by ID, and listPendingTransfers() lists them by creation time. Pending state records work this device still owes. The cloud represents what other devices should see. The UI can show progress early, but sending finishes only after the cloud steps succeed. A retry keeps the message ID so it can recognise an earlier successful commit. # Sending a file files/send registers a placeholder, uploads the attachment and then replaces the placeholder with the final file message. The placeholder has type file-uploading and a pendingAttachment , without a final DriveItem ID. Other devices can show it immediately. The final message keeps the same ID. The attachment goes under files/year/month/message-ID/original-filename , so two messages can carry files of the same name. Once upload returns a DriveItem , replaceMessage() commits type: "file" to the original chunk with an ETag check. The ETag is the server’s version marker: the check makes sure nothing else has modified the target chunk in the meantime. Part two covers concurrent writes in detail. Failure point What happens next Placeholder registration Try to remove a possibly written placeholder and return upload-failed . Attachment upload fails or is cancelled Try to remove the placeholder and retain failed local state for follow-up. Upload succeeds but final commit fails Return reconciling , keep the attachment details and allow a commit retry. files/retry-commit rebuilds the message from the existing attachment. If the final record already exists it returns it, without uploading again. These are separate writes; a later failure doesn’t roll back an earlier success. The intermediate state tells the client whether to retry the transfer or just the commit. There’s a month-boundary edge case. Attachment paths use the request’s createdAt , but message writes obtain the target month with getUtcMonth() at call time. A long upload or retry across midnight at month end can separate the two. Version 1.0.3 doesn’t pin one immutable month context across the whole send. # Upload sessions and chunks Once you select a file, the UI hands the upload to the runtime on your device. The runtime handles authentication, transfers and storage. Extensions dispatch to the background runtime; the native iOS app uses its own entry point. Small files can be passed as Base64 and written to the target’s /content endpoint using HTTP PUT . Larger files stay as Blobs in shared IndexedDB. The runtime creates a Graph upload session with createUploadSession and sends successive slices to its dedicated URL, avoiding a large Base64 round trip. # Selecting a transfer method and chunk size On slower connections, each completed chunk lets the client update the progress bar with the number of bytes OneDrive has accepted. If a chunk fails, only that chunk needs to be retried. Regular chunk sizes use Graph’s 320 KB alignment; the final chunk carries the remainder. OneDrop chooses 320 KB, 640 KB or 5 MB, respectively one, two or sixteen base units. Non-images larger than 4 MB use 5 MB chunks; other files of at least 1 MB use 640 KB; smaller files use 320 KB. Smaller chunks report progress sooner; larger ones reduce request count. shouldUseUploadSession() starts using sessions at 320 KB. That threshold is OneDrop’s choice. MAX_DIRECT_FILE_BYTES = 4 * 1024 * 1024 guards the direct upload function and helps select chunk size. Neither value is an overall attachment size limit. # Validating and submitting chunks Direct upload checks the decoded byte count against the file size; session upload checks the Blob size. For direct uploads, directory preparation and content transfer each have a twelve-second budget. Otherwise directory requests could use up nearly all the time before the upload even starts. User cancellation and timeout return distinct errors. Creating the session requires a Graph token. After that the client sends slices directly to uploadUrl with Content-Range: bytes start-end/total . The end is inclusive, hence end - 1 in the code. A partial upload normally returns 202 Accepted . A saved file returns 200 OK or 201 Created with the resulting DriveItem . The client validates its ID, name and size, constructs the attachment metadata and marks progress complete. If all local chunks have been sent but no completion response arrives, it reports an error. Sending the last byte alone doesn’t establish that Graph saved the file. # Retrying and recovering progress Each chunk gets up to three attempts with waits of 500 milliseconds and one second. Although the code lists 429 and several 5xx statuses, errors enter the same catch block and other non-cancellation exceptions can also retry. It doesn’t use Retry-After . Cancellation aborts the current request with AbortController . A manual resend checks for an existing file at the original path with the same name and size. It can reuse that object, but doesn’t compare content hashes. Progress includes acknowledged bytes, the current chunk end and historical average speed. The UI uses that average to estimate progress. Failing to read or write local speed statistics doesn’t stop the transfer. The loop doesn’t persist the upload URL or offset or query the server for missing ranges after a restart, so closing the program can’t resume the session at its last chunk. # Downloads and file reuse # Download addresses and image previews OneDrop looks up @microsoft.graph.downloadUrl by DriveItem ID, then delegates to the platform. The URL is temporary. The persistent message stores the ID. For inline image previews it can also read /content , Base64-encode the bytes and embed them in a data URL for the UI. This preview path has a 4 MB limit, checked after reading the content. Ordinary uploads and downloads have separate rules. # Reusing a download The desktop extension maps cloud DriveItem IDs to browser download IDs. On reopening, it checks whether the download still exists, finished or was interrupted. It reuses a valid entry and discards a stale one before downloading again. Save As and forced downloads bypass reuse. openExistingDownload() returns false for a missing record, removed file or interrupted download. An active transfer returns its status; a completed one records the new open operation. # Confirming completion browser.downloads.download() receives the URL, filename and options such as whether to show Save As. Its returned downloadId identifies a started browser task. It’s independent of the cloud driveItemId . The client removes control and path characters from filenames and handles name collisions. It calls browser.downloads.search({ id: downloadId }) to check for in_progress , complete or interrupted . A completed file that still exists can be registered; interruption returns an error. For an active download it adds a browser.downloads.onChanged.addListener() callback, which receives the browser task ID and the properties that changed. OneDrop filters events by ID and queries the full task state again. It removes the listener once the outcome is known. A download can finish between the first query and listener registration. If the new listener misses that notification, the UI can wait for a download that has already finished. An immediate second query closes that gap. In the code, finish() queries the state and handles the result: browser.downloads.onChanged.addListener(onChanged);// Check the current download state again after registering the listener.void finish();Only a confirmed completion saves the mapping for reuse. An ordinary download interrupted with FILE_EXISTS gets up to three attempts to find an available name. Save As leaves the failure for the user to handle. A file already saved on the user’s device remains theirs when a cloud message is removed. At this point messages and attachments are on OneDrive. Part two follows what happens when other devices read and modify them, and how archives and deleted records are maintained.

title: OneDrop: Sending Text and Files through OneDrive
text: OneDrop is a tool I built so you can send text and files between your devices through your own OneDrive. This post covers why I made it, where it’s available and what I’d like to improve. I left the implementation details for a separate post. I’ve since written them up in part one and part two of my series on storage and sync. # Why I made OneDrop I use Edge on pretty much everything. It came with Windows and I got used to it, so even on my Mac and phone I install it and make it my default browser. Edge’s built-in Drop used to be how I moved things between devices. I used it all the time. When a later version of Edge removed the feature, I wanted to keep that habit going. I could send files to myself in WeChat, and there’s no shortage of file transfer tools. But most of the time I’m just passing a link, a bit of text or an attachment to another device. Opening a separate app always felt like one step too many. Edge is usually open already. I wanted to be able to send the item right there and get on with what I was doing. # Why OneDrive I didn’t want to run a server just to move things between my own devices. The cost and maintenance didn’t make sense for this use. Since I was building for Edge, using a Microsoft account and OneDrive felt natural. Many Edge users already have an account. You sign in with your own account and the text and files stay in your own OneDrive. There’s no separate storage service for me to maintain. A Microsoft account includes 5 GB of free cloud storage, shared with other content on the account. That’s normally enough for my snippets and occasional files. If your OneDrive is already pretty full, check the space available first. # What it’s like to use Text and file transfers share a single message list. On desktop Edge the extension opens in the sidebar, so I can use it without leaving the page. That’s the experience I wanted to keep: send something here when I need it on another device, then pick it up there. You can go back through your message history. I wanted long-term archiving too, so OneDrop could match Drop’s features as closely as possible. The free 5 GB can fill up. OneDrop lets you delete individual messages and has a recycle bin, so you can keep the records you want and remove the rest. Deleting a message from the list removes its record there. To finish deleting it and reclaim the storage, clear it from the recycle bin too. # Where it’s available The desktop extension is available from the Edge Add-ons store. Mobile installation takes more work. Edge has a submission process for mobile extensions. I submitted the Android and iOS forms, but at the time of writing I hadn’t received a reply to either. The desktop store installation route doesn’t work for them yet. For early access, the GitHub release includes a CRX package. It requires developer mode and the corresponding test browser: Edge Canary on Android or the TestFlight version of Edge on iOS. The installation guide lists the steps. They don’t carry over directly to stable mobile Edge. On iOS there’s also an IPA for the native application. It’s intended for import into LiveContainer, which you need to set up first. It isn’t an App Store build or something you can install by tapping the download. # Rough edges and plans The hurdle I notice most is still installation on mobile. The desktop version has a store listing, while both a test browser and LiveContainer need extra setup. That’s an awkward first impression for a tool I made to save myself a few steps. I’ll keep an eye on the mobile extension submissions. I’ve also considered a standalone Android app, but I haven’t set a date. For now I want to get the everyday operations right: sending, viewing and clearing items across devices. The source is on GitHub. If you have similar habits, the installation requirements are a good place to start. At the time of this post, the project had reached 1.0.3. Most features were in place and had been through an initial round of testing. If you run into anything, leave a comment or open a GitHub issue.

title: Managing Projects with Git and GitHub
text: Git records versions. GitHub hosts repositories and provides a place to discuss issues and review code. Knowing how to use both is a basic development skill. Pushing code is only one step. A typical change also raises questions about branches, commits, review, automated checks and release. This post follows one change through that process. # Organising a repository # What belongs in the README? When you open a project for the first time, you want to know what it does, what’s working so far, and how to run it. A README should answer those questions up front, then point you to the docs for more detail. A useful order is introduction, demo, main features, installation or startup, contributing and licence. For a graphical application, one real screenshot often conveys more than a long feature list. Include the prerequisites and commands someone needs to install dependencies and run it. In my DungeonTavern README, I start with the project and documentation links, show the actual scene, then cover features and startup. Long design notes can live in separate documents. Relative links to files and screenshots continue to work when readers switch branches or download the source. # Explain usage and contributions The licence describes permitted uses. A CONTRIBUTING.md can explain environment setup, validation and contribution submission. Link both from the README. Templates make these reports more consistent. An issue template can ask for reproduction steps. A pull request template can ask what changed and how the contributor checked it. # Exclude files that don’t belong in history Use .gitignore to exclude files you don’t want under version control. A Node.js project might ignore installed dependencies, build products and local configuration: node_modules/dist/.env.env.*!.env.exampleKeep only variable names and dummy values in .env.example . Whether to track dist/ depends on distribution: some repositories intentionally version their built output. Adding an already tracked file to .gitignore won’t untrack it. To remove it from the index and keep the local copy: git rm --cached .envOld commits still contain it. Revoke or rotate a secret that was committed. # Create a branch for the change Check for unfinished local changes first, then create the working branch from an up-to-date main branch. The example assumes a main branch named main and a remote named origin : git statusgit switch maingit pull --ff-only origin maingit switch -c fix/category-wrap--ff-only stops if local and remote histories have diverged. That gives you a chance to inspect both sides. Use a name that describes the change, such as fix/category-wrap or feat/search . Keep a release script edit separate from a category layout fix so each can be reviewed, reverted and located in history independently. Short-lived branches suit many small projects; version branches become useful when maintaining multiple release lines. # Bring in changes from main Commit your work in progress or stash it. Once the working tree and index are clean, fetch: git fetch originChoose one of these approaches according to the project’s conventions: # 在当前工作分支中合入主分支git merge origin/main# 或者，把当前工作分支的提交重放到新的主分支之后git rebase origin/mainA merge preserves the existing commits and can join diverged histories with a merge commit. A rebase replays changes on a new base and gives the replayed commits new IDs. Situation Approach Reason Others share the branch or work on top of it Prefer a merge Their existing commit IDs remain valid. The work is entirely local A rebase is reasonable Nobody else depends on the old IDs. The branch was pushed but only you use it Follow the repository convention Updating the remote after a rebase usually requires a force push. Check who depends on it first. The target requires linear history Use a compatible rebase, squash or fast-forward A merge commit would violate the rule; a fast-forward creates none. Coordinate before rewriting shared history. Don’t rewrite a public main branch simply to sync your work. Choosing a PR merge method below concerns a later step. Resolve conflicts in the files, then mark them resolved with git add . Complete the merge commit or run git rebase --continue as appropriate. To abandon the operation, use git merge --abort or git rebase --abort . Restore stashed changes with git stash pop ; restoring can itself cause conflicts. Run the relevant checks even after a clean textual merge. # Organise changes into commits Inspect the changes before committing: git statusgit diffgit add -pgit diff --cachedgit diff shows unstaged changes and git diff --cached shows what the next commit will contain. Stage selected hunks with git add -p ; add new files separately after checking status. Implementation, tests and documentation can belong in one commit when they accomplish one thing. Splitting mechanically by file makes less sense than separating unrelated formatting, debugging files and behaviour changes. Mixing those together makes reverting the functional change much harder. For a public project, English commit messages can help contributors who speak other languages. Follow existing language conventions. Git itself doesn’t require English. Describe the effect of the change, with context where needed: Fix wrapping of long category titles on mobileAllow titles to wrap within the text column instead of movingbelow the date.Once you’ve checked the staged changes, run git commit and enter the message in your editor. A subject like the one above tells you what changed when you browse the history. An entry like update or fix bug leaves you guessing. The Git project’s contribution guidelines also ask contributors to group changes logically and explain why they made them. Prefixes such as feat: and fix: are a team convention and can help generate release notes. Use them if they suit the project. What matters is that the messages are clear and consistent within the repository. If you’ve just committed and discover a related change you left out, stage it and run the following while the commit is still unshared: git commit --amendAmending changes the commit ID. If others already depend on it, adding a follow-up commit is usually easier than rewriting history just to tidy up the message. # Open and merge a pull request Push the working branch and establish its upstream: git push -u origin fix/category-wrapOpen a PR against the intended base. Explain the problem, the change and how you verified it. Here’s an example description: ## 改动修复手机端分类长标题换行后挤开日期的问题。## 验证- 检查长标题和短标题的排列。- 检查桌面与窄屏下的分类跳转。Closes #42Only list checks actually performed. Verify that Closes #42 points to the issue this change resolves. Use a draft PR to discuss an unfinished approach. Review existing behaviour and edge cases as well as the new code. Push follow-up fixes to the same branch; the PR updates automatically. The VS Code contribution guide asks contributors to keep PRs focused and avoid unrelated formatting, which makes changes easier to review. # Choose a merge method Syncing the working branch during development and deciding what history lands on main are distinct decisions. A branch rebased locally can still be squash-merged. A branch kept current with merge commits can also be squashed. GitHub option Result on the target When it fits Create a merge commit Keeps the branch commits and adds a merge commit The full branch relationship is worth retaining. Squash and merge Records the PR as one new commit Many small fixes together form a single change. Rebase and merge Replays the commits individually, with new IDs and no merge commit The separate commits already tell the intended story. Follow the project’s convention. # Clean up after the merge After confirming the merge, remove the remote working branch if appropriate and update local main. A squash of commits A, B and C produces a new S on main. A merge commit keeps A, B and C and joins them with M. git branch -d checks ancestry against the tracked upstream, or against the current branch if there’s no upstream. It doesn’t compare resulting content. A squash-merged branch can therefore report not fully merged . Confirm the PR landed and that the working branch has no later unmerged commits. Only then, if needed: git switch maingit branch -D fix/category-wrapCapital -D skips the ancestry check. Removing the local branch reference doesn’t undo the squash commit. # Automating checks and releases with GitHub Actions Running a PR’s build and tests automatically gives reviewers a result and a log for every update. # CI/CD Continuous integration means integrating code frequently and running automated builds and tests to catch problems early. For example, a project can build and run its tests on each PR. Continuous delivery also prepares a releasable package, with release potentially left to a person. Continuous deployment sends passing changes to production without that final approval. These are workflows made up of concrete operations such as testing, building, uploading and deploying. GitHub Actions can orchestrate them, and can also perform unrelated repository tasks such as applying labels. # Add a check workflow Store workflows under .github/workflows/ . Events such as pushes, PR changes and manual dispatch trigger workflows. Each workflow contains one or more jobs. Each job runs on a runner, and its steps run commands or invoke actions in order. Use needs to express dependencies between jobs. For this example the project uses Node.js 24, has a committed package-lock.json , and defines CI-compatible test and build scripts in package.json . Create .github/workflows/ci.yml : name: CIon: pull_request: branches: [main] push: branches: [main] workflow_dispatch:permissions: contents: readjobs: check: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v6 - uses: actions/setup-node@v6 with: node-version: '24' cache: npm - run: npm ci - run: npm test - run: npm run buildThis workflow only checks the application. It runs on PR updates and checks main after a merge. For manual dispatch the workflow must already exist on the default branch. npm ci installs from the lockfile. If there’s no test script, substitute the project’s actual check command. When strict action pinning is required, use a verified full commit SHA. In Actions, open a run and find the first failing step. Its context distinguishes dependency installation, test and build failures. This actual OneDrop CI run includes formatting, TypeScript compilation, tests and two build targets: # Caches, artifacts and releases cache: npm reuses npm’s package cache, not node_modules ; the workflow still runs npm ci . Artifacts preserve results such as installers or test reports for later jobs or downloads. A separate release workflow might trigger from a tag, a published release or manual dispatch. Deployment environment protections can require approval where the repository and plan support them. The check example needs only contents: read . Grant additional permissions only to jobs that need them. Put tokens in Secrets. External fork PRs have restrictions on tokens and secrets: avoid executing untrusted PR code in a privileged pull_request_target context. # Protect main GitHub offers classic branch protections and rulesets. Multiple rulesets can apply alongside existing protections. The table uses the English labels from Rulesets. The classic branch protection page groups and names its options slightly differently. Rule Purpose Require a pull request before merging Route changes through a PR. Require status checks to pass Require named checks such as CI. Required approvals Set the approval count within the PR rule. Block force pushes Protect existing history. Restrict deletions Protect the branch from deletion. Require linear history rules out merge commits on the target. Select compatible squash or rebase merges. See GitHub’s ruleset reference. Run a workflow at least once before selecting its check name. Path filters or conditional jobs can otherwise leave a PR waiting for a check that never appears. For a solo project, avoid requiring approvals nobody can give; larger projects can add reviewers or code owners. Also check plan availability and who can bypass a rule. # Contributing through a fork With write access, push a working branch to the project. Otherwise fork the project on GitHub, clone your fork locally and propose changes upstream. Forking creates a hosting relationship; cloning downloads a repository. After cloning your fork, origin generally points to it. Add a remote for the original project, commonly called upstream . These names are conventions. Replace OWNER and REPOSITORY with the original project’s owner and name. If upstream already exists, verify its URL instead of adding it again. git remote -vgit remote add upstream https://github.com/OWNER/REPOSITORY.gitHere main follows upstream and personal changes stay on working branches. Handle uncommitted work first, then sync: git fetch origingit fetch upstreamgit switch maingit merge --ff-only origin/maingit merge --ff-only upstream/maingit push origin maingit switch -c fix/category-wrapBoth fast-forward checks can stop on divergence between local main, your fork and the original repository. Inspect the unique commits and decide what to keep before merging or rebasing. A force push would rewrite history without answering that question. Create a working branch, make the change, push to your fork’s origin and open the PR against the branch requested by the project. Read the contribution guide for the target branch, tests and whether an issue discussion is expected first. # Managing large files with Git LFS Images, models and audio sources may need versioning alongside code. Git LFS stores small pointers in Git and keeps the contents in LFS storage. GitHub rejects ordinary Git files over 100 MiB. Consider LFS for required versioned binaries, ignore build caches and put downloadable release installers in Releases. Once you’ve installed Git LFS, initialise it in the repository and add a tracking rule. Here’s an example for PSD files that ordinary Git hasn’t tracked yet: git lfs installgit lfs track "*.psd"git add .gitattributesgit add assets/example.psdgit commit -m "Track PSD assets with Git LFS"git lfs ls-filesgit lfs track writes the rule to .gitattributes . Commit that file so collaborators use the same rules. Check git lfs ls-files to confirm the files are managed by LFS. Collaborators need Git LFS too. If a checkout contains only pointer text, run git lfs pull . Adding a tracking rule doesn’t shrink existing history. Migrating old binaries rewrites commits: back up, define the scope and coordinate with collaborators before doing so. Check the account’s storage and download allowances as well. # Tagging a version After confirming the exact release commit, create and push an annotated tag: git tag -a v1.0.0 -m "Release v1.0.0"git push origin v1.0.0A GitHub Release builds on a tag with release notes and downloadable assets. Document visible changes, fixes and upgrade requirements. Attach built installers separately; an automatically generated source archive isn’t the compiled application. # Undoing changes Run git status and git diff first to see which changes you want to keep. Situation Command Effect Reselect staged changes git restore --staged path/to/file Keeps working-tree edits. Discard unwanted unstaged changes to a tracked file git restore path/to/file Restores the index version and discards those edits. Reorganise the most recent unshared commit git reset --soft HEAD~1 Removes the commit from the branch tip while retaining staged changes. Undo an ordinary commit on a shared branch git revert COMMIT Adds an inverse commit and preserves history. The default mixed reset also resets the index but keeps working-tree changes. A hard reset overwrites affected working-tree changes too. Reverts can conflict; reverting a merge requires deciding which parent is the mainline. Fixes and reversions on public branches can go through the same branch, PR and check process.

title: Customising My Zsh Prompt
text: Oh My Zsh manages Zsh configuration and comes with themes, plugins and some handy defaults. I originally picked Zsh and Oh My Zsh because I wanted a better-looking terminal. I tried a lot of the bundled themes. Most were too busy for my taste, and the simpler ones weren’t quite what I wanted either. Eventually I wrote my own. Here’s the theme I use, how the prompt works and which plugins I’ve kept. # My current prompt The theme itself is six lines: PROMPT="%{$fg[cyan]%}%c%{$reset_color%}"PROMPT+=' $(git_prompt_info)%(?:%{$fg_bold[green]%}%1{%} :%{$fg_bold[red]%}%1{%} )'ZSH_THEME_GIT_PROMPT_PREFIX="%{$fg_bold[blue]%}git:(%{$fg[red]%}"ZSH_THEME_GIT_PROMPT_SUFFIX="%{$reset_color%} "ZSH_THEME_GIT_PROMPT_DIRTY="%{$fg[blue]%})"ZSH_THEME_GIT_PROMPT_CLEAN="%{$fg[blue]%})"The first line shows the final directory component. The second adds the Git information and status symbol. The last four set the Git prefix, suffix, and indicators for clean and modified working trees. I deliberately gave DIRTY and CLEAN the same value. The base theme shows the branch without distinguishing local changes. # Installing a custom theme Oh My Zsh’s customisation conventions support themes under $ZSH_CUSTOM/themes . With the default installation, that’s ~/.oh-my-zsh/custom/themes . Keeping a separate .zsh-theme file makes it easy to find and edit later. Create the directory, respecting a custom value of ZSH_CUSTOM if you have one: mkdir -p "${ZSH_CUSTOM:-$HOME/.oh-my-zsh/custom}/themes"Save the six lines as sycamore-simple.zsh-theme , then edit the existing ZSH_THEME setting in ~/.zshrc . Omit the filename extension: Put it before source $ZSH/oh-my-zsh.sh so it’s in place at initialisation. Open a new terminal to check the result. # Understanding the configuration If you’d rather start with a few examples, skip to common variations and come back when you want to change a particular detail. # What controls the prompt? Oh My Zsh uses ZSH_THEME to find the file and supplies helpers such as git_prompt_info . Zsh variables and prompt expansion determine what gets drawn. Variable When it appears PROMPT / PS1 Main prompt waiting for input. Both names refer to the same parameter. RPROMPT / RPS1 Right-hand prompt while editing a command. PS2 / PROMPT2 Continuation prompt for unfinished input, such as a quote or loop. RPS2 Right-hand continuation prompt. PS3 Selection prompt in a select loop. PS4 Prefix on execution trace lines. Most themes concentrate on the first two. Here are examples for continuation, selection and debugging: PS2='%_> 'PS3='请选择编号：'PS4='+%N:%i> 'In PS2, %_ names the unfinished shell construct; if you see this prompt after Return, the command needs more input. PS3 affects select menus. In PS4, %N and %i show the script or function name and line number. Use set -x to start tracing and set +x when finished. # Prompt expansion reference Zsh expands percent sequences when displaying the prompt. This is a selection from the prompt expansion manual. Purpose Sequences Display Directory %c Last component, with home abbreviation Directory %~ Full path with home or named-directory substitutions Directory %/ , %d Full path without home abbreviation Identity %n , %m , %M Username, short hostname, full hostname Terminal %l , %y Terminal name with different prefix handling Status %? , %j , %L Exit status, job count, shell nesting level Privilege %# Hash for a privileged shell, percent otherwise History %h , %! History event number Time %T , %* 24-hour time without or with seconds Date %D{%Y-%m-%d} Formatted date Colour %F{cyan} / %f , %K{black} / %k Set/reset foreground and background Style %B / %b , %U / %u , %S / %s Start/end bold, underline or standout Literals %% , %) Percent sign or closing parenthesis A number before a directory escape limits the component count: %2~ keeps the last two, useful if you want the project name without filling the line. The PS2 and PS4 examples above show how to use %_ , %N and %i . Related debugging escapes include %^ for unfinished constructs in reverse order, %x and %I for the defining file and line, and %e for evaluation depth. For a two-line prompt put a literal newline in the string or concatenate $'\n' . In ordinary single quotes, backslash-n remains two characters. Format Meaning %t , %@ 12-hour time with am/pm %D , %w , %W Two-digit year-month-day, abbreviated weekday and day, or month/day/two-digit year %D{format} A strftime-style format, e.g. %Y , %m , %d , %H:%M:%S The codes inside date braces have their own meanings. Zsh adds unpadded day ( %f ), 24-hour ( %K ) and 12-hour ( %L ) fields. Fractional seconds use %. ; %6. requests six digits, %9. or %N nine. Actual precision depends on the clock. Forms such as %-d suppress padding. Other extensions depend on the system. %E clears from the cursor to the end of the line. %{...%} encloses nonprinting sequences such as colour codes so they don’t count towards prompt width. Keep ordinary text outside this wrapper. Inside such a sequence, %G accounts for one visible character cell and %2G for two. The older %c and %. show the final directory component, and %C does the same without abbreviating home as ~ . The manual deprecates the older directory forms %c and %. in favour of %1~ , and %C in favour of %1/ . I kept %c above to show my actual theme. A function can compute values first and leave formatting to the prompt using the psvar array. %v selects the first item, %2v the second; negative indices count from the end. With psvar=(demo) , %v displays demo. # Conditional output The second line of my theme uses %(?:success:failure) to change the final symbol between green and red according to the previous exit status. Add %? to display the numeric status itself. The question mark selects the test. The two colons separate test, true branch and false branch. Both can instead be dots, as in %(?.success.failure) . In the general form %(test.true.false) , the comparison value nnn can appear before or after the opening parenthesis; it defaults to zero. Test True when ! The shell has privileges. # , g Effective user or group ID equals n. ? Previous exit status equals n. _ At least n shell constructs are open. / , C The absolute path has at least n components; root counts as zero. c , . , ~ The substituted path has at least n components. D , d , w Month, day of month or weekday equals n. Months are zero-based; Sunday is zero. T , t Hour or minute equals n. e , j , L Evaluation depth, jobs or shell level is at least n. S SECONDS is at least n; this is not the previous command’s duration. v , V psvar has at least n entries, or its nth entry is set and nonempty. l At least n characters have been printed on the line; a negative argument tests space left to the opposite edge. For example, %(!.#.>) displays a hash for a privileged shell and a greater-than sign otherwise. Choose another delimiter if your branch text contains a dot. Use %) for a literal closing parenthesis in a branch. Conditionals can nest. Negative condition arguments use their absolute value except for the remaining-width form of l . # Dynamic information The Git branch changes while the shell stays open. I put $(git_prompt_info) inside the prompt so command substitution runs the helper each time the prompt is displayed. This requires: setopt PROMPT_SUBSTOh My Zsh already enables this option. For a standalone test you’ll need to enable it; the colour variables and Git helper still come from Oh My Zsh. Quoting controls when substitution happens: # 设置时保留函数调用，每次显示提示符时再执行PROMPT='$(git_prompt_info) '# 设置时立即执行函数，保存这一次返回的结果PROMPT="$(git_prompt_info) "Single quotes keep the call for the next prompt expansion. Double quotes evaluate it when assigning the variable. I used single quotes for the Git helper and the battery and Python examples below. # Common variations Each example starts with my six-line theme and changes one thing so you can compare the results. # Show the full path Replace the first line of the theme with the following to show the full path: PROMPT="%{$fg[cyan]%}%/%{$reset_color%}" To show your home directory as ~ , replace %/ with %~ . Both keep the full directory hierarchy. # Show the username To show the username and hostname before the path, append this line to the theme: PROMPT='%n@%m '"$PROMPT" If you only want the username, replace %n@%m with %n . # Put the time on the right Append the time to the left prompt after loading the theme: PROMPT+=' %F{yellow}%*%f 'Or keep the space between directory and input free by setting the right prompt: RPROMPT='%F{244}%D{%H:%M:%S}%f' Choose one. The battery and Python examples also assign RPROMPT; assigning it again replaces the previous value. The time is evaluated when the prompt is displayed. It isn’t a continuously ticking clock, and the right prompt gives up space as the command line grows. # Show the battery level Here’s the macOS example. Put the function and right prompt after the theme: sycamore_battery() { local value value=$(pmset -g batt 2>/dev/null | sed -nE 's/.*[[:space:]]([0-9]+)%;.*/\1/p' | head -n 1) [[ -n $value ]] && print -rn -- "bat ${value}%%" return 0}RPROMPT='$(sycamore_battery)' Without battery information it displays nothing. The %% in the function’s output becomes one percent sign during prompt expansion. The query runs on prompt refresh, without a background polling task. # Show the Python project, environment and version If you switch between Python projects and environments often, you can show the project marker, environment name and interpreter version in the prompt. Place this function and right prompt after the six theme lines: sycamore_python() { local env_name version text='' [[ -f pyproject.toml || -f requirements.txt ]] && text='Python project' if [[ -n $VIRTUAL_ENV ]]; then env_name=${VIRTUAL_ENV:t} elif [[ -n $CONDA_DEFAULT_ENV ]]; then env_name=$CONDA_DEFAULT_ENV fi [[ -n $env_name ]] && text+=" env:${env_name}" if [[ -n $text ]] && (( $+commands[python3] )); then version=$(python3 --version 2>/dev/null) text+=" ${version}" fi print -rn -- "${text//\%/%%}" return 0}RPROMPT='$(sycamore_python)' It checks the current directory for pyproject.toml or requirements.txt , reads the environment from VIRTUAL_ENV or CONDA_DEFAULT_ENV , and reports the version of python3 on PATH. It doesn’t search parent directories or read version-manager configuration. If prompt refreshes are frequent, cache the version after changing environments instead of launching an interpreter every time. # Mark a dirty Git working tree I gave clean and dirty trees the same suffix in the original. Change DIRTY to add an asterisk when the tree has changes: ZSH_THEME_GIT_PROMPT_DIRTY="%{$fg[blue]%}) *" Oh My Zsh handles status detection; its settings affect whether untracked files count. Run git status to see the actual changes. # Plugins These are the six plugins enabled in my setup: plugins=(git zsh-autosuggestions zsh-syntax-highlighting z extract web-search)Put this in .zshrc before Oh My Zsh initialises. The theme defines the prompt; plugins add commands and input behaviour. Install a plugin before adding its name. # git Adds shortcuts such as gst for git status and gco for git checkout . The theme’s git_prompt_info helper comes with Oh My Zsh independently of this plugin. # zsh-autosuggestions Shows suggestions after the cursor, using command history by default. After running python test.py , typing the beginning can suggest the rest. The upper line has suggestions turned off. In the lower line, grey text is the suggested part awaiting acceptance. # zsh-syntax-highlighting Colours the input so commands, arguments, quoted strings and some invalid input are easier to distinguish. The input highlighting is separate from the directory colour in the prompt. # z Jumps to previously visited directories. Once you’ve visited a project folder, z followed by part of its name can find it. # extract extract filename chooses the decompression tool for the archive type. I like having one command for the lot. # web-search Commands such as google zsh prompt open a query in the browser, handy when looking something up from the command line. # Fonts and rendering My default iTerm profile uses JetBrainsMonoNFM-Regular at 12 points. Select a font with the appropriate glyphs in your own terminal. If the  icon appears as a box, switch fonts or simply replace it with > in the theme. Width matters too. My theme declares %1{%} as one cell. If the terminal draws it two cells wide, the cursor can end up in the wrong place.
